# ASSUMPTIONS: everything a ptxv verdict rests on

A ptxv verdict ("clean", "race", ...) is a theorem *relative to* the assumptions below. This
file is the single registry of them. Rules:

* Every assumption has an ID. The code that relies on it carries an `ASSUME(ID)` comment, and
  every verdict lists the IDs it depends on (`assumes:` in `ptxv check` output and in
  `summary.md`). `cargo test` fails if this file, the registry in
  `crates/sim/src/assumptions.rs`, and the code tags disagree.
* **Status** is one of:
  - **enforced**: checked at runtime; violating inputs give `unmodeled`, not a silent answer;
  - **validated**: tested against GB300 or a cross-check, with the evidence named;
  - **argued**: justified from documentation or reasoning, but not tested;
  - **refuted**: tested against GB300 and false; kept (opt-in) only so that old verdicts can
    be reproduced, and listed in their `assumes:`;
  - **unvalidated**: chosen for convenience; may be wrong.
* **If wrong** says which way the verdict fails:
  - a *miss* means we could call a buggy kernel clean (unsound);
  - a *false alarm* means we could report a bug that cannot happen (incomplete).
* Features the model does not cover are not assumptions. They fail loudly: an unknown SASS
  opcode is a hard error, and an unmodeled operation or value gives a finding of kind
  `unmodeled`, which makes the verdict inconclusive.

Kinds: `code` assumptions are tagged in the source; `process` assumptions are about how we test
and are not tagged.

---

## E: execution model (how schedules are explored)

### E-SPIN · code
**A failed `mbarrier.try_wait` blocks the thread until the mbarrier changes** (instead of
returning false and letting the thread do something else).
- Where: `exec.rs` `try_wait_result`, `split_enabled`; checked by `spin.rs`.
- Status: **enforced** (2026-10-30). `spin.rs` proves, for every try_wait on both front-ends,
  that blocking is exact:
  - the instructions before the retry branch are register-only, do not read the result, and
    keep the poll operands;
  - the failure path only re-polls the same mbarrier with the same operands (plus no-ops and
    branches);
  - every successful re-poll rejoins the continuation.

  Any other shape gives an `unmodeled` finding (fixture r0 B49). All fixture binaries pass.

  **Undefined poll values** (MISS 40, 2026-11-10): a poll iteration is tried on a copy and
  blocks while it would fail; the copy read never-written shared memory as 0 (spin again) and
  its S-INIT finding was dropped with it. A poll on a flag nothing initialized was clean on
  both fronts and under `--certify`, while GB300's garbage shared memory ends the spin at once
  (`fixtures/s_smem_acquire` without the flag's zeroing: 50/50 wrong, 3 of 4 words stale).
  A blocked poll (scalar or warp-level) whose flag bytes nothing has written is now reported
  where it blocks (`spin::blocked_poll_read` / `blocked_wpoll_read`, sig `uninit-poll:<pc>`);
  the poll still blocks until a write. Pinned: `s_smem_acquire` NOINIT (violation on both
  fronts, also under `--certify`); source mutant `spin-undef-block` reverts the fix and is
  caught.

  A warp-poll dry run is accepted only when execution raises no error or finding and
  preserves both the bytes and definedness of every store as well as all participating
  lane and uniform register state. Otherwise the real step runs, retaining its diagnostic
  (`spin.rs` `wpoll_dry`; `execution_reduction_tests`). An uninitialized mbarrier wait or
  peek likewise reports its first `mbar-uninit` diagnostic before parking, including a
  peek forced into blocking mode (`mbar_uninitialized_wait_reports_before_blocking`,
  `mbar_uninitialized_peek_reports_before_parking`,
  `mbar_uninitialized_forced_peek_preserves_the_diagnostic`).

  **Compare-and-swap update loops** (2026-11-06, ptxas's loop for `atom.add.noftz.bf16`:
  `H: new = f(old); got = ATOMG.E.CAS [a], old, new; P = got != old; old = got; @P BRA H`) are
  not polls and are not blocked: the model runs every iteration as a step. That terminates in
  every schedule, since a failed attempt reads a value another thread wrote after this
  thread's previous read of the location, and the writes are finite. probes/bf16x2 (two such
  loops) = GB300 bitwise. Since 2026-11-12 (MISS 174, forum post 76: the same loop for
  `atom.add.noftz.f16`, `ATOM.E.CAS` on a generic address) the recognizer is exact and shared
  with E-CAS-SEED (`ptxv_ir::casloop::cas_retry_loop`): a 32-bit CAS; one block of
  unconditional register-only operations; the one write of the compare register in the loop
  is a plain copy of the CAS's returned value after the CAS (`MOV` / `IMAD.MOV`; an add or a
  constant is not); the branch predicate is written once, by `old != cmp` (or `==` under
  `!P`) after the CAS and before the copy, so only a failed compare repeats; the back branch
  is a plain per-thread `@P BRA` (not `@P BRA.U`, where a failed lane leaves when a warp-mate
  succeeded; not `@P BRA Q, L`, where it leaves when Q is false; not `BRA.DIV`, where a lane
  that succeeded goes round again; accepted until review RHA, 2026-11-12; ptxas 13.0 emits only
  the plain form in every CAS loop seen); no address register is written in the loop; nothing
  else is carried. Before, any refresh computed from
  the returned value alone was accepted (`cmp = old + 1`, a loop waiting for a value) and the
  exit predicate was not checked. Pinned: `spin::cas_tests` (ptxas 13.0's loop, its `ISETP.EQ` /
  `@!P` and `MOV` forms and a {compare, new} pair accepted; refused: a compare refreshed from a
  constant, from `old + 1` or from another register, or overwritten before the CAS; an exit on a
  value, on a second predicate too, on success, tested after the refresh, or a predicate written
  twice; an exit branch with `.U`, a second condition or `.DIV`; the returned value rewritten after the CAS; the address moving or recomputed in the
  loop; another carried register; a predicated operation or a load in the loop), fixtures
  `e_cas_retry` (SASS and PTX) and `e_atom_half`.

  **Loops whose exits do not test a strong load** (2026-11-06): a strong load inside a loop
  makes it a poll only if the loop's exit depends on the loaded value. With a conditional back
  branch the branch's predicate is tested (DeepEP's `ld.volatile` copy loops); with an
  unconditional back branch, every exit of the loop (`EXIT`, a branch out of it) is, by a
  forward register-taint dataflow over the loop's control flow and back edge to a fixpoint
  (`spin::loop_exit_tainted`; an unguarded write from untainted operands clears a register,
  a guarded one changes nothing). A loop none of
  whose exits depends on the value terminates without other threads' writes, so the model
  runs its iterations as steps (Triton's pipelined main loop in
  `_kernel_dispatch_and_calc_grads` reads a `volatile` word each iteration and stores what it
  read; it was reported `unmodeled`). Fixture e_vol_loop: `good` explores clean, `SPIN` (exit
  on the loaded value) and `CARRY` (exit on a counter that adds the loaded value each lap)
  keep the `unmodeled` finding (tests/reductions.rs). Memory flow is
  not followed (a loaded value stored and re-read), as in the conditional case.

  **Warp-level poll loops** (rung 4b, DeepEP `barrier_block` and channel waits): a loop whose
  body branches forward, reconverges (`BSYNC`), checks convergence (`BRA.DIV`), votes and
  loads, but writes no memory, with a strong load inside and a back branch to its head
  (`spin::wpoll_loops`). The split at the head runs one iteration on a copy
  (`spin::wpoll_dry`): if every member comes back to the head with unchanged registers and
  predicates, the iteration is a stutter step and the split blocks; its loads are recorded
  for the race detector and as its DPOR footprint (`blocked_poll_read` analogue). The first
  iteration, which changes registers, runs for real. Clock timeouts inside need E-CLOCK.

  **Recomputing retry stubs** (rung 2): ptxas may recompute the parity into a free register
  at the head of the out-of-line retry stub (`R4 = UR6 << 31; w2: TRYWAIT [a], R4`). This is
  accepted when the stub prefix is straight-line, unguarded and register-only, `w2` polls the
  same mbarrier with the same result predicate, and every register the prefix writes is dead
  at the continuation (`spin::live_after`, predicate-aware). Whether `w2` polls the same phase
  is checked whenever the original poll succeeds: the stub runs on a copy of the thread
  (`check_stub_parity`); a different phase gives `unmodeled`.
  The stub may also poll through a register computed between the wait and its retry branch
  (FA4: `TRYWAIT [UR10+0xc0]; ...; UR6 = UR10+0xc0; @!P0 BRA stub`, stub `R2 = UR6; TRYWAIT
  [R2+URZ]`): that segment is pure (`spin::retry_branch`), so `check_stub_parity` runs it
  first, with the poll's predicate false as on the retry path, then the stub, and compares
  the mbarrier address and parity as before.

  **Peeks** (rung 2, CuTeDSL): CUTLASS tests an mbarrier early (`try_wait` into a predicate),
  does other work, and later skips or runs a blocking wait loop depending on the result. Such
  a try_wait does not have the retry shape, but it is now run as what it is: a non-blocking
  test that returns false while the phase is pending (`Machine::peeks`). It qualifies when,
  assuming it and every other peek fail, every path from it back to itself passes a
  retry-shaped (blocking) try_wait (`spin::is_peek`, which tracks the result predicate). A
  success is progress, so a peek cannot spin without the mbarrier moving. A path back to the
  test that passes no blocking wait also qualifies when none of its branches and side effects
  depends on a failed result (forward dataflow from every assumed-failed result, guards
  included; a store or other side effect reading one counts as a dependence): the same path is
  taken when the test succeeds, so that loop is the kernel's own, not a wait (2026-11-07;
  FA bwd Sm100, BlackwellFusedTopkSelection: a test before a tile loop whose empty case skips
  the result; fixtures/e_peek_loop good, and SPIN, whose loop repeats while the test fails,
  stays `unmodeled`). Other try_waits without the retry shape are still blocked on and
  reported `unmodeled` (fixture r0 B49).
  (rung 3b) The walk also follows the result through a token register: trtllm-gen keeps it
  as `SEL R4, RZ, 0x1, !P1` and later decides with `ISETP.NE.AND P1, PT, R4, 0x1` whether to
  wait (known predicates and registers from SEL with constant operands and integer EQ/NE
  compares). A warp vote into a predicate (`VOTEU.ANY UP0, P1`, then `USEL` of the token;
  trtllm-gen bmm `schedS ... lbW2`) of a known predicate is that predicate: under the walk's
  assumption every lane's test fails, and every known value is lane-uniform (built from
  failed results and immediates); a vote is not a side effect (fixtures/e_peek_loop VOTE,
  clean; VOTESPIN, whose loop repeats while the vote is false, stays `unmodeled`). A try_wait
  whose result goes to `PT` (trtllm-gen polls the next stage ahead of
  time) is lowered as a no-op: it does not block, writes nothing, and dropping its acquire only
  removes happens-before edges (it may add a race report, never hide one).
  **Peeks in DPOR (`PTXV_EXPLORER=dpor`).** A peek is enabled before and after the completion
  it reads, with different results, so DPOR must schedule both orders. Its success acquires the
  completion as an observation (`Footprint::obs`): ordered after it in the trace taken, but
  not skipped by the race check. Until 2026-11-12 every acquire was skipped, so DPOR explored
  only the outcome its first schedule happened to give (MISS 221; `probes/dpor_testwait`, no
  remote operations: good [clean] on both fronts and RACE PTX [clean] against the stateful and
  `--certify` [nondeterministic] / [nondeterministic, race]).
  **Blocking waits in DPOR.** The race check skips, for a blocking wait, the updates that
  released what it acquires: every one comes after the completion of the previous phase and
  before the observed one, where the wait is blocked. Where the acquired generation cannot
  come round again (named barriers, bulk groups, the cluster barrier, an mbarrier's first
  phase or its init) it also orders their history before the wait. A parity poll that
  acquired a later phase is enabled two phases earlier too, and at init for parity 1, so
  there only the releasing updates are skipped (dpor.rs header, "Co-enabledness of polls";
  `Footprint::acq_aba`). Until 2026-11-12 the race check ordered the releasers' history
  before every wait (it joined the releaser's whole clock), so DPOR missed schedules in which
  a parity wait passes in an earlier phase (MISS 230; `probes/dpor_aba_wait`: good PTX
  [clean] against the stateful [race], SASS [clean] against [nondeterministic]; also with
  test_wait spins and suspend-time hints).

  **Poll loops on strong loads** (rung 1f, `spin::poll_loops`): a loop
  `H: ...; r = ld.strong [a]; ...; @p bra H` whose body is otherwise register-only (plus
  acquire fences) and carries no register from one iteration to the next is run only when the
  iteration exits: `split_enabled` tries the step on a copy. A failed iteration changes nothing
  a later one does not overwrite, so this is exact. A strong load inside a backward branch's
  range with any other shape gets an `unmodeled` finding.

  **Poll loops on plain loads** (2026-11-02, fixture `e_spin_smem`): ptxas compiles
  `ld.acquire.cta` / `ld.relaxed.cta` / `ld.volatile` of shared memory to a plain `LDS`, so a
  shared-flag spin is a plain-load loop in SASS (plain `ld` spins in PTX likewise). Plain
  loads are not scheduling points (E-DRF), so such a loop used to run inside one transition
  until the 10M-instruction local-step limit, never seeing the other warp's store (a `fault`
  verdict after minutes; a racy poll also pushed one race finding per iteration, which grew
  memory without bound). A plain load with exactly the poll-loop shape above is now blocked
  the same way: the step that reaches it stops there while the iteration would fail. Plain
  loads in loops of any other shape (reductions, carried counters) are not polls and are not
  listed or reported. A failed iteration only re-reads the flag, so skipping it is exact
  for registers and control; for the race detector, a split that stops at a poll that would
  fail (strong or plain) reads the flag once, without effect on registers and without
  acquiring (`spin::blocked_poll_read`). The polling thread synchronizes with nobody while it
  spins, so every later write of the flag by another thread is checked against that read as
  it would be against the skipped iterations: a race unless both are morally strong. A poll
  that never succeeds is a reported deadlock. (Not acquiring from a failed read's writer can
  only add races.) On SASS, LDS/STS are relaxed strong at CTA scope (S-SMEM-STRONG), so a
  shared-flag handoff that ptxas kept in order is clean, as on GB300.

  **Compare-and-swap polls** (2026-11-03, rung 4a, torch symmetric memory): the signal
  `while (cas(&pad[i], 0, 1) != 0);` / `while (cas(&pad[i], 1, 0) != 1);` compiles to
  `H: R6 = 0; YIELD; [MEMBAR.ALL.SYS]; CAS R0, [R2], R6, R7; [CCTL.IVALL]; ISETP; @P0 BRA H`.
  It is a poll loop of the shape above with the CAS as the poll operation (`AtomOp::Cas`; a
  failed compare is a read only, so a failed iteration changes nothing), a release fence
  allowed in the body (repeating it after attempts that wrote nothing publishes nothing new),
  and loop-invariant prefix writes (`R6 = 0`, recomputed identically) not counted as carried.
  The exiting iteration's CAS swaps and writes. Blocked CAS polls read the flag for the race
  detector and the explorers' footprints like a blocked load poll. Validated on GB300 by
  `fixtures/s_cas` (bitwise; its lost-signal mutant hangs, as the model's deadlock says).
  The certificate (E-WELLSYNC) covers CAS signals with C-CAS (below): a put and its wait
  are not HB-ordered, but the values force their order (2026-11-03).

  **Retries that loop back to the poll's own prefix** (2026-11-02, rung 3a CUTLASS grouped
  GEMM): `H: R3 = R2 << 31; R0 = UR5; w: try_wait [R0], R3; @!P0 nanosleep; @!P0 re-poll;
  @P0 EXIT; BRA H` (an `@d EXIT` decides: the exit is the continuation) and `H: R2 = UR7; w:
  try_wait [R2+0x40], R73; ...; @!P0 BRA H`. The retry path (after unconditional branches)
  runs register-only straight-line code back into `w`, rewriting poll operands. Accepted
  with a run-time check: on every successful poll the executor reruns `H..w` on a copy and
  requires the same mbarrier, the same parity, and every register unchanged (the prefix is
  what the thread ran before its first poll), so skipping the retry is exact; otherwise
  `unmodeled` (`spin-parity`). Tests: `crates/sim/tests/spin_shapes.rs`.
  **Peeks in the explorer (`explore.rs` `peekwait_set`, `peekskip_set`; `PTXV_NO_PEEKWAIT`
  turns both off, `PTXV_NO_PEEKSKIP` the second).** A peek races with the arrival that
  completes the phase it reads, so the stateful explorer branched on every such order,
  though CUTLASS's peeks only decide whether a later blocking wait runs. Two model changes
  make a peek's outcome invisible where that is provably all it decides. They apply only in
  the explorer (`explore_one`); the certificate (E-WELLSYNC) keeps the plain model.
  - *Peek as one blocking wait (`peekwait`).* The shape is `d = try_wait [A], P`, then
    register-only code, then `@d bra J`. The failure side has register-only code (not
    touching the poll's operands), then a try_wait with the same operands and the retry
    shape, then `@!d bra` to its retry, falling through to J. Every register the failure side
    wrote (other than `d`) is dead at J. The peek is then run as that blocking wait: it is
    disabled while the phase is pending, as a failed try_wait is under the spin model. A
    failed peek followed, with no effect, by a wait that blocks until the phase completes
    and joins J with the same live registers is exactly that. r3: 7 of the epilogue's 17
    peeks (`d040`/`d060` and its siblings).
  - *Peek as a failed test (`peekskip`).* For CUTLASS's "test now, work, then wait": the
    peek's result decides, maybe through derived predicates (PLOP3, ISETP's combining
    predicate, VOTE) and across loop iterations, whether a later blocking wait on the same
    mbarrier runs. Two worlds are walked in lockstep from the peek, `d` true in one and
    false in the other:
    - instructions reading nothing that differs run alike in both, whatever their effect;
    - a branch on a differing value must agree, or the failure world goes alone through
      register-only code, blocking try_waits and other peeks to where the success world
      went;
    - registers still differing there must be dead.

    Then every behaviour of the success world is one of the failure world (it waits where
    the other skipped, and the wait passes at once), so the peek is run as a test that
    fails. Two things are checked at run time, else the verdict gets `unmodeled`:
    - *Same wait:* the skipped wait is on the peek's mbarrier and parity
      (`peekskip-target`).
    - *No ABA:* the mbarrier completes no phase while the window from the peek to the
      worlds' join is open and the test would pass (`peekskip-aba`: then the success world
      went on while the failure world waits a phase longer). A failed test reads no phase,
      so it no longer depends on the completion it races with. Its footprint reads only
      the key of that ABA completion, so the explorer runs both orders of exactly that
      completion, and the check sees it.

    A peek whose lanes disagree on its guard runs as before, and so does one whose result
    skips no wait (its success also acquires, which a failed test would not). r3: 10 more peeks (producer
    `3df0`/`4060`/`4140`/`42f0`, MMA `82e0`/`85c0`, scheduler `93b0`, epilogue
    `b740`/`b7a0`/`b7c0`).
  - Racy kernels: a search that finds a race is run again without the peek changes (a note
    says so). Under E-DRF the reductions do not keep the outcomes of racy kernels, and the
    peek changes removed branching that happened to expose some of them (r2_cute_gemm CM1:
    `nondeterministic` disappeared).
  - Soundness check: `PTXV_CHECK_WALKS` runs its random executions in the changed model
    (every end state must be one the explorer reached), then again in the plain model,
    comparing terminal outputs and findings (end states differ in dead registers and in
    where a deadlocked thread waits).

### E-CAS-SEED · code
**The plain load that seeds the first compare of a CAS retry loop can be modelled as a relaxed
load of the CAS's scope when its value reaches nothing but that compare.** ptxas emulates a
16-bit atomic add (`atom.add.noftz.f16` / `.bf16`, sm_100 / sm_103 have no native form) as
`LD.E Rcmp, [Ra]` of the containing 4-byte word, then a CAS retry loop on the word. As a plain
load it races with every other atomic on the word (MISS 175, forum post 76).
- Applied only when exactly (`ptxv_ir::casloop::seed_load`, SASS front, `cas_seed_loads` in
  `crates/sass/src/lib.rs`): the loop is a CAS retry loop (E-SPIN's exact recognizer); the
  nearest write of the compare register before the loop head is an unconditional plain,
  coherent 4-byte load of it, in the CAS's state space, from the CAS's address (same base
  registers and offset; the CAS is 4 bytes, so one aligned word); between the load and the loop
  head only unconditional register-only operations or a `BSSY`, none reading the compare register or
  writing an address register; no branch, `brx` target or call return lands between the load
  and the loop head except the loop's own back branch (`CALL.ABS` reaches only
  `__assertfail`, a trap).
- Argument: the value can only become the first attempt's compare, and the loop exits only on
  a successful compare, so whatever the load returns (stale, torn, any bits) the loop's effect
  is the same atomic read-modify-write of the word, at the cost of at most one failed attempt.
  A relaxed load returns a subset of those values, so no outcome is dropped. A conflicting
  plain write by another thread is still reported at the CAS, which follows the load with only
  register operations in between (nothing that synchronizes).
- Not applied (the load stays plain and races): the loaded value also used elsewhere (stored,
  compared, carried past the loop head in another register), a different address or width, a
  CAS loop that does not refresh its compare from the returned value or exits on anything but
  the compare (`e_cas_retry` variants, `casloop` tests).
- Not covered: the 16-bit atomic's 4-byte accesses can reach 2 bytes past an allocation sized
  to the last 16-bit element (in the containing word). That is reported (`fault`: outside the
  case's allocation), though GB300 does not fault inside an allocation granule. Since
  2026-11-12 the warp-mates of a faulting thread are no longer left parked on it at a
  reconvergence point or barrier (no derived `deadlock`): on GB300 a fault aborts the grid
  (probes/fault_abort), so nothing waits for a faulting thread (`exec.rs`
  `release_after_stop`, fixture `e_atom_half` `exact_size`). What the other threads do after
  that release is no GB300 execution and need not end (MISS 235: r4c_nowrap B36's dispatch
  warps go round a named barrier a faulted warp no longer holds back), so the certificate's
  run stops at a step that stops threads at an error and does not hold (`wellsync.rs`
  `run_logged`; the explorer decides; probes/cert_fault_stop).
- Where: `crates/ir/src/casloop.rs`, `crates/sass/src/lib.rs` `cas_seed_loads`.
- Status: **argued** (2026-11-12). The loops' SASS shape is ptxas 13.0's for sm_103a
  (`fixtures/e_cas_retry`); probes/half_add runs both emulated atomics on GB300 (one thread per
  word, values bitwise).
- If wrong: a *miss* of a race on the seed load's word (only if a load outside the recognized
  shape were rewritten).
- Retire: when ptxas emits a strong load for the seed, or the race detector learns to discard
  a read whose value is validated before use.

### E-ALLOC · code
**A `tcgen05.alloc` that cannot succeed blocks until columns are freed.** ptxas actually emits
a `UTCATOMSWS` + `NANOSLEEP` retry loop. Who else holds columns: E-TMEM-COTENANT (opt-in).
- Where: `exec.rs` `split_enabled` (TMEM alloc blocking).
- Status: **argued** (same structure as E-SPIN; the retry loop is visible in the SASS).
- If wrong: *miss*, as for E-SPIN.
- Retire: the same static retry-loop check, applied to the alloc loop.
- Guardrail race (2026-11-10, not an assumption): ptxas's tcgen05 guardrail code frees the
  columns (`UTCATOMSWS.AND`) before it clears its shared-memory bitmap (`ATOMS.AND`), so a warp
  that allocates in between traps at its dealloc. The SASS front reports it at both levels
  (fixtures/e_tmem_alloc_block good). GB300: none in 1.18e9 contended pairs of the unmodified
  code (probes/tmem_alloc_race), every launch traps with the window widened by 32-64 ns
  (probes/tmem_alloc_race_wide). A GB300 exemption was considered and rejected: only timing
  hides the race.

### E-DRF · code
**DRF-SC reduction:** plain loads/stores and TMEM accesses are not scheduling points. Only
synchronization operations interleave; races among plain accesses are found with vector clocks.
- Every operation on synchronization state other actors observe is a scheduling point,
  `mbarrier.inval` / `SYNCS.CCTL.IV` included since 2026-11-12: it was run eagerly inside a
  step, so its order against an init, arrival, wait or store at the same address in another
  warp was explored one way only (a `SYNCS.EXCH.64` re-init unordered with it was clean on
  SASS; MISS 242, fixtures/e_mbar_store_order REINITU, probes/mbar_store_order).
- Where: `ir` `Op::is_visible`, `explore.rs`.
- Status: **argued.** This is the standard theorem for the core scoped PTX model. Its extension
  to the async, tcgen05 and tensormap proxies is assumed (docs/design.md §9).
- If wrong: *miss*, for a racy kernel whose bad outcome needs an interleaving of plain
  accesses. The race itself is still reported, so a clean verdict stays correct as long as the
  theorem holds for race-free programs.
- Retire: a litmus campaign for the proxies (docs/design.md §7.2).

### E-CTA-REP · code
**A CTA whose position-dependent control values equal a representative's behaves as the
representative does, up to its global addresses** (`ptxv check --certify --rep`;
docs/grid-cost.md reduction 1; 2026-11-07). A CTA's execution is a function of its position
(`%ctaid`), of values equal in every CTA (parameters, `%tid`, constant banks, E-CLOCK's clock)
and of the bytes it loads. For a representative CTA r three runs of r's slice decide:
- a data run (num.rs taint with every global byte a source, `Taint::all_global`): no guard,
  control operand or address depends on loaded data; a comparison excused by N-FMAX or
  N-FINITE refuses;
- a position run (num.rs taint, every special register that can differ between CTAs the
  source: `SReg::position_dependent`, as E-CTA-INDEP's symmetry check): every
  position-dependent guard, control operand (`Taint::trace`'s points) and global address
  operand (`pos_free_regs`, and a cp.async source) is recorded with the dataflow graph of the
  per-thread register instructions that computed it from `%ctaid`, every other operand a
  constant;
- the certificate (E-WELLSYNC) on r's slice; a representative that stands for no other CTA is
  explored instead when it does not certify.
For every other CTA c the graph is replayed on c's corresponding threads by the instructions
themselves (`Machine::exec_pure`, so `%ctaid` reads c's position). If every recorded control
value equals r's, c takes r's path: by induction over the path, every other control value is
position- and data-independent, hence equal. So c has r's synchronization, shared-memory
addresses and global accesses, at its replayed addresses. c's verdict is r's when its accesses
also overlap each other exactly as r's do (the same pairs: the same races and orders under the
same happens-before) and lie in their allocations. An address outside every allocation is a
`fault` finding of c. Across CTAs, a byte one CTA writes and another accesses is a `race`. This
is more conservative than the explorer, which keeps S-SAME-VALUE writes as notes. A CTA whose
control values differ joins a later regime with its own representative (at most `PTXV_REP_MAX`,
default 16).
- Refusals: the launch is then checked as before, with the cause in a note
  `E-CTA-REP refused: ...`. Causes: a multi-kernel launch; clusters of more than one CTA;
  multicast, NIC or multi-GPU memory; data-dependent control or address; a global atomic or
  strong access; a position-dependent value through memory or a cross-lane operation (vote,
  match, redux, R2UR); TMA coordinates that depend on the position; a global access completing
  after its instruction; S-SAME-VALUE in a representative; a non-certified representative that
  stands for other CTAs; more than `PTXV_REP_MAX` regimes.
- Outputs: only representatives run, so the launch's outputs are not assembled or compared.
  A representative explored alone with several outputs makes the launch `nondeterministic`
  (the counts multiply).
- Position sources (2026-11-08, soundness harness): `SReg::position_dependent` (ir) is the
  one classification, an exhaustive match: `%ctaid`, `%clusterid`, the cluster shape
  (`SR_CgaSize`) and `%warpid` (the warp's SM slot on hardware) always; the cluster rank,
  `%cluster_ctaid` and shared-window addresses when a cluster has more than one CTA. Until
  then only `%ctaid` seeded: `%clusterid` (equal to `%ctaid` in 1-CTA clusters) could decide a
  fault in one CTA that the representative did not show (PTX certified clean), and the
  symmetry check let cluster 0 stand for a cluster whose output depends on the schedule
  (PTX `--slices` clean). Also until then the launch kept one output when a representative's
  exploration had several (both front-ends: `nondeterministic` dropped). fixtures/e_pos_sreg
  (tests/reductions.rs `position_through_other_special_registers`).
- Value faults (2026-11-09, soundness harness, num.rs `value_fault_operands`). A register
  instruction can fault on a value: an integer division's divisor (zero), `cvta.to.shared`
  (outside the window), a constant-bank load's base (past the bank), an `IADD3` with one
  carry-out (a carry of 2). Those operands are control for the taint runs: a data-derived one
  refuses in the data run (and N-EQUIV's precondition), and in the position run an
  instruction with a position-dependent one is a replay root, replayed for every CTA, where a
  fault makes the replay refuse. Until then they were data: a `div.s32` by input data (or by
  `%ctaid - 3`) zero only in CTA 3 was clean with --rep. fixtures/e_rep_divzero (good, DATA,
  POS, CVTA, LDC; tests/reductions.rs `value_faults_keep_their_class_under_cta_reductions`);
  every pure operation is classified (`every_pure_op_is_classified_for_value_faults`).
- Where: `rep.rs` (hooks in exec.rs `exec_traced` and `access_x`); CLI `--rep` (PTXV_REP=1).
- Status: **argued**. It relies on the replay reproducing c's values: every instruction of the
  graph is a per-thread register instruction (num.rs `pure_op`, cross-lane ones excluded) whose
  sources and old destinations are set before it runs, and a recorded node whose register
  changed by a write the log did not see is not replayable.
- Evidence: fixtures/e_cta_rep. good: 2 representatives for 8 CTAs (CTAs 0-6, the tail CTA 7),
  clean. TAIL1 (the tail stores past the end): fault. AND and STRIDE (CTAs write each other's
  elements): race. N1024 (CTA 7 is never simulated and stores past the end: its replayed
  address): fault. DATACTL (a branch on loaded data): refused, decided by the fallback. Each
  mutant has the full certificate's classes on both front-ends (tests/reductions.rs).
  Measured: triton `_finish_block_lanes` (5000 CTAs) and quack rmsnorm 4096x8192 (4096 CTAs)
  each certify with one representative.

### E-INPUT-INDEP · code
**Input coverage's provenance covers every flow of input bytes into the guards, branch
conditions, addresses and synchronization operands of the run it records** (coverage.rs;
2026-11-09). Input coverage (`ptxv check`, on by default) runs the launch once with a
provenance shadow: every global byte the launch starts with is input, and values carry the
input allocations they derive from through registers, shared, global and local memory, TMEM,
warp-collective operations (every lane's operands) and guards of register arithmetic (the
destination carries the guard's provenance). `input_independent`: the run finished and no
guard of a non-arithmetic instruction, branch condition, address or synchronization operand
derived from input data. Then the control path, the accesses and the synchronization of that
run are the same for every input of the same kernel binary, launch shape and parameters.
- Used by: the printed "input-independent: holds for all inputs of this shape and these
  parameters".
- Scope: one schedule's provenance. In a certified run (E-WELLSYNC) every schedule reads the
  same values, so the per-thread data flow is the run's. Value-dependent parts of a verdict
  (same-value writes, output determinism, the comparison with the GPU output, the numerics'
  value-range findings such as an MMA operand outside the calibrated range) hold for the
  captured input only.
- Coarse places, over-approximating (never dropping provenance): an MMA reads every written
  byte's provenance; TMEM is one set; a spilled input-derived value makes every local load
  input-derived; a CTA-wide barrier reduction carries every input-derived predicate.
- Where: coverage.rs (`pre`, `post`, `ProvState::on_access`); main.rs (the printed claim).
- Status: **argued**. Evidence: the soundness harness's dead mutants (of 242, none lies behind
  an input-dependent condition); the differentials of docs/input-coverage-cost.md.
- If wrong: *miss* (input-dependent control reported as fixed).
- Retire: a static data-flow proof of input independence over the whole program.

### E-RACE-DEAD · code
**A race whose racing loads' values reach nothing has no effect on the outcome** (class
`race-dead`: kept as a finding with its GB300 label, no verdict class; 2026-11-07). A
read-write race is a plain or relaxed load by a thread that happens-before does not order with
a write; the load may return either value. The check is run again with every racing load
(thread, pc) of the race leaving its destination registers undefined (`Machine::dead_probe`),
and S-INIT reports any undefined bit that reaches a store, an address, a predicate or branch,
an atomic or synchronization operand (so also every output). If the rerun reports no finding
the first run did not, and ends as it did, the loaded value reaches nothing on any explored
path, so a load of the other value leaves the same events; otherwise the race stays `race`.
Applied only when the races are the check's only failing findings (no violation, fault,
deadlock or unmodeled finding; one output for the explorer): a run that already reports
undefined values cannot show that the racing loads add none (a use of a never-written
location has the same signature as a use of a probed load; fixtures e_elect B46,
e_stasync SA2), and the rerun must report no failing finding at all.
- Which loads: `Machine::race_log` records every racing read of every explored transition
  (exec.rs, before the per-instruction deduplication of findings), shared by every copy of the
  machine; the decision needs a complete exploration (or the certificate's run, which covers
  every schedule). A race with another kind of read side (write-write, an atomic, an
  acquiring load, which synchronizes with what it reads, an asynchronous unit) stays `race`.
- Tensormap proxy fences (2026-11-09): the read of `fence.proxy.tensormap::generic.acquire`
  (SASS `UTMACCTL.IV`, `Op::TmapFence`) counts as a racing read too. Its only value is the
  snapshot of the 128 map bytes that later TMA ops compare against (`tmap_at`: the thread's own
  snapshot, or one of a thread of the CTA that happens-before the use); the fence has no
  register destination and its ordering effect does not depend on what it read. The probe run
  leaves that snapshot undefined (no bytes), so every TMA op that relies on it reports a stale
  map (`tmap-fence`), a failing finding, and the race stays `race`; when no TMA op relies on
  it, both values of the read leave the same events. A CuTe distributed grouped GEMM's
  dispatch kernel: every epilogue warp runs `fence_tensormap_update` on the C map while
  only warp 0 publishes and uses it, so warps 1..3's fences race with warp 0's
  `tensormap.cp_fenceproxy` (`ATOMG.E.EXCH`) and are value-dead. Fixture
  `e_race_dead_tmap` (good: race-dead, clean, explored and certified; TF1: thread 32 also
  TMA-loads with the map it fenced, the race stays).
- The racing reads come from the search whose verdict is returned. When a race makes
  the explorer search again (without the value-insensitive polls or the peek changes), the
  race log is cleared first (2026-11-07). The first search's value-insensitive acquire polls
  acquire nothing, so they logged reads that the returned search orders. That made
  fixtures/l1_litmus neg-payld a race in exploration but race-dead in the certificate.
- Mixed-size data races (MISS 226, 2026-11-12): a race whose two operations overlap partially
  stays `race` on the PTX front, dead value or not. PTX ISA 9.5 section 8.7.2: "A data-race
  between operations that overlap completely is called a uniform-size data-race, while a
  data-race between operations that overlap partially is called a mixed-size data-race. The
  axioms in the memory consistency model do not apply if a PTX program contains one or more
  mixed-size data-races. But these axioms are sufficient to describe the behavior of a PTX
  program with only uniform-size data-races." A data-race (8.7.1) counts weak accesses too, so
  a plain byte load of a word written concurrently is one. Without the axioms nothing says
  which values the racing load returns or what else the program does, so a loaded value that
  reaches nothing does not give the same outcome. For a uniform-size race the axioms hold, the
  load returns one write's value, and the rule stands. `Machine::race_log` records no read for
  a pair not known to be one location on the byte (`overlap_at`, S-SCOPE's complete overlap:
  two thread instructions whose element sizes differ, weak or strong, and a thread's access of
  another size than the NIC's element, MISS 194; a CQE access the fields do not decide,
  `Overlap::Unmodeled`, counts as not one), so the signature has no entry and stays `race`. A
  signature is the other access's pc and the kind, so a uniform-size race that shares one with
  a mixed-size race stays `race` too (conservative).
  - Placement: ISA text, so the strict level (`ptx_contract`) of the PTX front, the only place
    overlap is decided (S-SCOPE). The SASS front's strict level, the GB300-profile re-run
    (`sass_gb300`, which runs the SASS front) and the level-2 hardware model that labels the
    strict level's races (twolevel.rs, `Launch::hw_order`) take every pair as one location and
    apply the rule as before: a SASS width is not a PTX element size (S-SCOPE), so a record
    checked on the SASS front only keeps a dead mixed-size race `race-dead` (S-SCOPE's SASS
    miss).
  - probes/race_dead_mixed (one command: `bash probes/race_dead_mixed/run.sh`): CTA 0 writes
    257 to a u32 word with `st.relaxed.gpu`; CTA 1 reads its low byte unordered and masks it to
    0 before storing it. good (`ld.relaxed.gpu.u8`) and PLAIN (`ld.global.u8`) were race-dead
    and clean on the PTX front until 2026-11-12, race now (no certificate); LIVE (the byte
    reaches a predicate) race before and after; SAME (`ld.relaxed.gpu.u32`, morally strong)
    clean without a race; UNIFORM (`ld.relaxed.cta.u32`) and UNIFORM_PLAIN (`ld.global.u32`),
    uniform-size races with the value masked, race-dead and clean before and after, explored
    and certified. fixtures/e_race_dead RDMIX (warp 1 loads one byte of the word thread 0
    overwrites): race on the PTX front (race-dead and clean before), race-dead and clean on
    the SASS front; good (uniform) race-dead and clean on both, as before. fixtures/e_nic_cta
    WORDDEAD (a 4-byte read of the 8-byte word an RDMA write lands, masked to 0) and CQEDEAD (a
    masked `.cta` read of CQE bytes 60-63, whose overlap with the CQE write is not modeled):
    race on the PTX front (race-dead and clean with MISS 194 alone). ptxas 13.0 drops the
    masked loads (the `and` with 0 folds and the store writes RZ), so those SASS rows have no
    race (toolchain). tests/reductions.rs `mixed_size_races_are_not_race_dead` (also the
    GB300-profile re-run and the hardware model); source mutants race-dead-mixed (the fix
    undone), race-dead-uniform-off (every pair kept out), race-dead-mixed-hw (overlap decided
    under `hw_order` too), race-dead-mixed-nic (the NIC's accesses not decided) and
    race-dead-unmodeled (an unmodeled CQE overlap taken as one location).
  - A/B (model; `--certify`, 2000 states, 1200 s): the fix against its int7 parent before MISS
    194 (865b2856) on every PTX-front kernel_db case (1197 PTX cases, 137 binary cases with PTX)
    and the 11 SASS records with race-dead findings. No kernel_db check changes: the flips are
    the repro's (good, PLAIN, RDMIX), and one tip run timed out at 1200 s where its base took
    1152 s (race, no race-dead finding: the fix cannot change it). The 39 checks with race-dead
    findings (28 PTX, 11 SASS) keep them all: no kernel_db kernel has a dead mixed-size race at
    these bounds. On MISS 194 (37e97477 against 9462af39) the 44 NIC records do not change. The
    40 checks with race-dead findings or a changed state, rerun on the final revs (int7 b9b4ecda
    against the fix, 1800 s), do not change either.
- Where: `race_dead.rs`; explorer `explore.rs` `explore_one` (a second exploration of the same
  model with the loads undefined); certificate `wellsync.rs` `run_logged` / `probe_run`
  (with C-ORDER's dead reads); the racing reads and the mixed-size exclusion: exec.rs, where
  races are recorded (`race_log`). DPOR (`--dpor`) does not apply it.
- Status: **argued** from the S-INIT semantics: a value that never reaches a sink cannot change
  memory, control flow or synchronization, so both values of the racing load give the same
  execution. Relies on S-INIT's sink coverage (its listed limits apply).
- Evidence: fixtures/e_race_dead: good (threads other than 0 load a word thread 0 then
  overwrites; warp 1 never uses it) is `race-dead` and clean on both front-ends, explored and
  certified; RD1 (warp 1 stores the value) stays `race`; RDMIX (a byte load) is `race` on the
  PTX front (tests/reductions.rs). Triton kernels
  that `tl.load` a scalar in every thread and store it from one lane:
  `_kernel_map_routing_global`, `_local_stats_partial_reduction`.
- If wrong: *miss*, for a use of the loaded value S-INIT does not report, and for a dead
  mixed-size race whose overlap is not decided (the SASS front, above).

### E-ELECT · code
**Which lane `elect.sync` / `ELECT` picks.** The PTX ISA says *"elects one predicated active
leader … deterministically, i.e. the same leader … for the same membermask"*, without saying
which lane.
- Where: `explore.rs` `actions`, `per_leader_policy`, `elect_sensitivity` (PTX),
  `elect_lanes.rs`, `exec.rs` `Op::Elect`, `wellsync.rs` `certify_runs`.
- Status:
  - **PTX front-end: the leader is a fixed function of the active set**, as the
    "deterministically" clause says, the same function for every warp. Which functions are
    explored is decided by a static gate (`explore.rs` `elect_sensitivity`, 2026-11-10): a
    flow-insensitive taint in which `%tid` / `%laneid` / lane masks / shuffles (not
    shfl.idx from a uniform lane) / match.any / atomics' old values, the
    lane-distributing loads (tcgen05.ld, ldmatrix, movmatrix, mma.sync fragments) and
    elect's lane number (the leader's identity itself) are lane-varying, and elect's
    outputs and what they reach (through data, collectives,
    memory, and the instructions a branch on them controls up to its immediate
    post-dominator) are leader-dependent. Sensitive: one instruction reading or running
    under both. The strict gate (`elect_sensitivity(m, true)`) adds a synchronizing
    instruction (barrier, mbarrier, fence, atomic, cluster barrier, cp.async / bulk wait,
    warp sync, tcgen05 commit and waits) reading or running under a lane-varying value, and
    any call, absolute call or indexed branch; where only it fires, the two policies decide
    and the verdict is qualified (E-ELECT-2POL below).
    - Memory: a load is leader-dependent when a write of leader-dependent data or address
      to its state space reaches it; lane-varying when its address or control is, or when
      it reads per-lane storage (local memory, tensor memory, a generic address) that a
      write of lane-varying data, address or guard reaches. tcgen05.mma, issued by one
      thread, reads whole tensor-memory tiles, not its lane's row (tcgen05.ld, which does,
      is lane-distributing). A load from shared, global or
      parameter memory at a warp-uniform address reads one location for every lane: the
      same value up to when each lane reads it, timing that the taint tracks for no value
      (**argued**). Kernel parameters and constant banks are their own space. What an
      instruction reads flows into what it writes (tcgen05.cp, TMA, atomics). Every
      operation says what it reads and writes (`explore.rs` `elect_mem_spaces`, a match
      without a default arm; `e_elect_mem_spaces_cover_every_op` classifies the fixtures'
      operation kinds independently): tcgen05.cp reads shared memory, tcgen05.mma shared
      memory and tensor memory, mbarrier arrivals and waits the mbarrier's shared words.
    - `%tid.x >> k` (k >= 5) and `%tid.x & m` (m clearing the low 5 bits) are warp-uniform
      when every block's x size is a multiple of 32, the register's single definition is
      the unguarded `mov` from `%tid.x` (the taint is flow-insensitive), and the instruction
      runs under warp-uniform control: written in a lane-varying branch's region, the lanes
      that skip it keep their old values. An indexed branch on a lane-varying index starts
      such a region too (fixtures/e_elect_tid_brx: the shift in a brx.idx target, PTX clean
      and certified before). The same holds for the collectives whose result is
      otherwise warp-uniform (vote.ballot, vote.all / any / uni, redux.sync).
    - A collective (ballot, reduction, shuffle, match) of a leader-dependent pattern
      (elect's predicate, values written under it), or one run under leader-dependent
      control, is lane-varying as well as leader-dependent: it can name the leader's lane
      (bfind of a ballot; shfl.idx from a fixed lane is set exactly when that lane leads),
      the leader's identity, as elect's lane number. vote.all / any / uni of it is the same
      for every leader and stays leader-dependent only.
    - sensitive: every leader function on the active sets a run meets, up to clones. The
      first elect of an active set branches over its candidate lanes, later elects of the
      set reuse that leader (`Machine::elect_fn`, hashed, sorted; `elect_any`). The
      certificate (E-WELLSYNC) runs once per explored function (each active set a run
      meets first spawns runs with each other candidate preset; at most PTXV_RING_MAX_RUNS
      runs, else no certificate). The verdict notes `E-ELECT: every leader function
      explored (...)` with the instruction.
    - Clones (`elect_lanes.rs` `lane_classes`): two lanes of every electing warp that no
      instruction tells apart (both execute it or neither; equal values, as functions of
      what each lane received, in every operand of an instruction with an effect), from a
      per-warp evaluation of the lane-dependent values (concrete where they are integer
      functions of the lane, else classes of equal values) to a fixpoint. Swapping two
      clones maps every execution with one as the leader to one with the other: the same
      outputs, the same findings up to the two threads' names. An active set's candidates
      are the lowest lane of each group of lanes nothing has told apart yet: one class, not
      a leader of an active set already met, in the same of those active sets
      (`elect_lanes::candidates`). Outside the analysis (every lane its own class): a call
      or indexed branch, elect's lane number read, a collective reading or run under a value
      elect's predicate reaches. fixtures/e_elect_mid: {0}, {1..30}, {31} (3 functions, as
      many as 32 give: `e_elect_lane_classes_match_every_lane`); e_elect_guarded_exit:
      {0, 31}, {1..30}. `PTXV_ELECT_CLASSES=0`: every lane its own class.
    - not sensitive: the lowest and the highest active lane as every leader, each run
      separately, verdicts merged (`per_leader_policy`). **Argued**: the leader's work reads
      and writes the same values and addresses whichever lane does it, so only the thread
      doing it differs; the two ends cover code that assumes lane 0 (e_elect B46) or that
      the leader is not a given lane. `PTXV_ELECT=fn` forces every leader function.
    Outputs that differ between leader functions make the verdict `nondeterministic`
    (implementation-defined under the ISA).
  - Fixtures (2026-11-10): e_elect_lane, e_elect_mid, e_elect_ldmatrix,
    e_elect_guarded_exit, e_elect_lane_number, e_elect_tid_redef, e_elect_tccp,
    r2_triton_gemm and r4_attn_triton explore every leader function;
    e_rmsnorm_cluster_drain (lane-varying cluster arrivals) is qualified E-ELECT-2POL; e_elect
    and the six r2 / r3 CuTe GEMMs pass both gates.
  - Before (2026-11-09 to 11-10) the deciding gate had no memory rules, and the strict gate
    fired on every CuTe GEMM through merged memory: one space for parameters, shared and
    global memory, tainted by any lane-varying store, so `ld.param` and the TMEM-address
    load were lane-varying. Both gates missed lane-distributing loads from a warp-uniform
    address (ldmatrix: each lane its own part) and code after a guarded `exit` / `ret` /
    `trap` in a branch's region (no fallthrough edge). fixtures/e_elect_ldmatrix and
    e_elect_guarded_exit race only for middle-lane leaders: PTX nondeterministic / clean
    then (two policies, qualified E-ELECT-2POL because the coarse memory rule fired), race
    now; SASS clean both times (GB300 elects lane 0). Until 2026-11-10 the taint took
    elect's lane number as leader-dependent only (MISS 49: a function of it equal at the two
    end lanes, fixtures/e_elect_lane_number), a shift by 5 of any register ever assigned
    `%tid.x` as warp-uniform (MISS 50: `%tid.x + 3` in the same register,
    e_elect_tid_redef), and had no read entry for tcgen05.cp / tcgen05.mma's shared
    operands, with writes taken before reads (MISS 51: the leader's ballot through tensor
    memory, e_elect_tccp): PTX clean for kernels racy for middle-lane leaders only, race
    now. Until 2026-11-11 a ballot of elect's predicate was leader-dependent but warp-uniform
    (MISS 71: bfind / popc of it gives the leader's lane, fixtures/e_elect_ballot) and
    `%tid.x >> 5` was warp-uniform wherever it was written (MISS 72: written on lanes 1..30
    only, fixtures/e_elect_tid_ctl), and shfl.idx of elect's predicate from a fixed lane
    was warp-uniform (MISS 79, fixtures/e_elect_shfl, also certified): PTX clean, race now
    (e_elect_tid_ctl also nondeterministic). From rung 2 to 2026-11-09 the two policies were used for
    every kernel: code correct for the two end lanes and wrong for a middle lane was
    reported clean, also under `--certify` (fixtures/e_elect_mid; a soundness miss of the
    PTX contract only, GB300 elects the lowest lane). Before rung 2 every active lane was
    explored at every elect, which is exact under no reading of the ISA (one warp could pick
    different leaders for the same mask); `PTXV_ELECT=all` keeps that mode.
  - A leader function that differs between warps, or between elects of one warp with the
    same active set, is outside the model (the ISA's "same leader for the same membermask").
  - **SASS front-end: validated.** It uses the lowest active lane, which GB300 picked for all
    8 active sets in `probes/elect` (2026-10-30).
  - A PTX membermask held in a register (DeepEP: `mov.b32 %r, -1`) is read when executed:
    every executing lane must hold 0xffffffff, else the record is refused (unmodeled). An
    immediate other than -1 is refused at lift. ptxas 13.0 drops the register (`ELECT P, UR,
    PT` even for 0xffff), so the SASS front sees a full-warp elect. probes/elect_regmask:
    GB300 20/20, both fronts bitwise (2026-11-08).
- Evidence: fixture e_elect B46 (code that assumes the leader is lane 0) is a race on PTX,
  clean on SASS, and correct on GB300. fixtures/e_elect_mid good (racy for the 30 middle
  leaders): race on PTX (explored and certified), clean on SASS.
  - ISA text: the leader is a deterministic function of the membermask, its lane unspecified.
  - GB300 measured: the lowest active lane (probes/elect, 8 active sets).
  - model (soundness audit, 2026-11-10): with the leader search off (the two end-lane
    policies for every kernel, the state before MISS 29's fix) e_elect_mid good / ENDS,
    e_elect_lane_number, e_elect_tid_redef, e_elect_tccp and e_elect_guarded_exit are clean on
    PTX (e_elect_mid also certified) and e_elect_ldmatrix loses its race; with it each gets its
    expected classes, explored and under `--certify`. Source mutants `elect-fn-off` (the
    explorer ignores the gate), `elect-fn-cert-off` (the certificate does), `elect-fn-lowest`
    (the search offers the lowest lane) and `elect-cand-ends` (an active set's candidates are
    its end lanes) are each killed by e_elect_mid.
  - model, kernel_db A/B (2026-11-11; leader search off vs on, PTX front, `--certify`, 1800 s
    per record and 300 s per fixture, 27 GiB) over the 136 PTX records whose deciding gate
    fires: no record with a verdict on both builds gains or loses a class (60 unchanged, 2 end
    incomplete at the state budget with the search), 58 end without a verdict on both builds,
    and 16 have a verdict on one build only: 6 no longer end in time with the search, 2 run out
    of memory where other builds with the search finish, and 8 reach a verdict where the build
    without the search (the two policies run one after the other) ran out of time or memory.
    The 23 records complete on both builds explore 10.6 to 16 times the states with the search
    (median 15.4). Fixtures: the 9 pairs of the fixtures above flip as listed, 18 are
    unchanged, 20 time out on both builds. Gate counts over a local PTX corpus: E-ELECT-2POL.
  - argued: the two-policy reduction where only the strict gate fires (E-ELECT-2POL), and
    the lane-class symmetry.
- Placement: the leader search is the strict level's (`ptx_contract`, PTX front): the ISA
  leaves the lane open. The SASS front and the `sass_gb300` level keep GB300's lowest lane,
  a measured rule (probes/elect), so MISS 29 and the taint misses 47-51, 71, 72 and 79 are
  PTX-contract only.
- The audit's two known gaps (2026-11-10; PTX front, silent: a function of the leader's
  lane computed from a ballot of elect's predicate, and `%tid.x >> 5` written under
  lane-varying control) are MISS 71 and 72, fixed (above).
- If wrong (SASS): *miss*, if a future chip elects differently. Re-run `ptxv probe probes/elect`
  on new hardware. If wrong (PTX: a leader-dependent value the taint misses, where neither
  gate fires): *miss* at the PTX contract only, a kernel racy or nondeterministic for
  middle-lane leaders reported clean.

### E-ELECT-2POL · code
**A PTX verdict reached with the two end-lane leader policies is conditional where only the
strict leader-sensitivity gate fires.** The strict gate (`explore.rs` `elect_leader_sensitive`,
reviewed by the soundness audit) adds to the deciding one (E-ELECT) lane-varying
synchronization (barriers, mbarriers, fences, atomics, cluster barriers, cp.async / bulk waits,
warp sync, tcgen05 commit and waits under or reading a lane-varying value) and any call,
absolute call or indexed branch. Where it fires and the deciding gate does not, the two
policies still decide what is explored, and the verdict lists `E-ELECT-2POL` and carries a note
`elect-2pol:<pc>` naming the rule and the instruction.
- Where: `explore.rs` `elect_two_policy_note`, `per_leader_policy`; `wellsync.rs`
  `certify_runs`; `assumptions.rs` `for_machine`.
- Status: argued (E-ELECT's two-policy argument). Exploring every leader function there
  costs up to 16 times the states (32 runs for 2), and lane classes do not reduce it in real
  kernels (lane-indexed accesses in the electing warps). Local PTX corpus (2026-11-10, 5090
  PTX entries with elect.sync): the deciding gate fires on 3745 (every entry the earlier
  narrow gate flagged, and 9 more from the two closed misses), only the strict gate on 995
  (992 lane-varying synchronization, 3 calls), neither on 350. Top first sites of the 995:
  Triton's `@(tid == 0) mbarrier.init` (320) and lane-varying `mbarrier.init` counts (97),
  `red.relaxed.shared::cta.min` under a lane guard (296 at three sites), and
  `mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx.shared::cluster` with a lane-varying count (104). Fixtures:
  e_rmsnorm_cluster_drain (remote arrivals by lanes 0 and 1).
- If wrong: *miss* (PTX contract only): a middle-lane leader the two policies do not stand
  for. GB300 elects the lowest lane, so the SASS / sass_gb300 level is unaffected.
- Retire (follow-up F-ELECT-SYNC): an argued exemption for lane-varying synchronization that
  runs before every elect and is separated from them by a full CTA or cluster barrier (the
  Triton `@(tid == 0) mbarrier.init` prologue), reviewed by the soundness audit, then the
  remaining sites explored with every leader function.

### E-CTA-INDEP · code
**Clusters (CTAs, without clusters) that share no synchronization object can be explored one
at a time.** When the kernel has no global atomics or strong global accesses, no executable
CLC (E-CLC eager launch) and a single grid, the stateful explorer only expands the lowest
cluster that can move (`explore.rs` `ctas_independent`, `cta_ample`). Cluster-scope
operations (DSMEM, remote arrivals, multicast TMA / commits, `cta_group::2`) only name CTAs of
the issuer's cluster; `griddepcontrol` is a no-op in a single grid.
- **Slices** (`ptxv check --slices`, equiv `slices = true`; `explore_sliced`): each cluster is
  explored in a machine where every other CTA counts as exited, and afterwards no global byte
  one slice wrote may be read or written by another (union over every explored transition,
  `GFoot`); otherwise a cross-cluster `race` is reported. With that, the slices' schedules
  interleave freely, so each terminal state, deadlock and race of the launch is one of a
  slice or a cross-slice conflict. Cost: per slice, not per launch (r2_cublas_gemm: 32
  clusters of 4 CTAs). Slices of warps across CTAs and GPUs, with a check over every
  footprint space: E-SLICE.
  A case with several launches is checked as launch groups instead (`--groups auto
  --slices`, E-LAUNCH-GROUPS): the cross-slice check knows no launch order, so it reported a
  stream-ordered (or PDL-gated) consumer's reads of its producer's output as cross-cluster
  races (`fixtures/r1e_pdl`; test `slices_keep_launch_order`).
- **Symmetry** (`explore_symmetric`, what `--slices` tries first): one deterministic run of the
  whole launch with the taint shadow in *position mode* (sources: `SReg::position_dependent`, `%ctaid`, `%clusterid`, ...; global addresses and
  TMA coordinates may depend on it). Every guard outcome and control operand value (shared /
  TMEM / mbarrier addresses, masks, counts) that depends on the position is recorded per
  thread; corresponding threads (CTA rank, thread index) of every cluster must have recorded
  the same sequence, and no global byte one actor writes may be accessed by another. Then
  cluster 0 is explored alone and stands for all. Argument: by induction over any schedule,
  cluster c and cluster 0 take the same steps with the same control values and the same
  shared/TMEM addresses (position-dependent values enter control only as recorded, and are
  determined by the thread's own path, or by shared memory written race-free exactly as in
  cluster 0); their global accesses never conflict with anyone's, so global reads return
  host data; so cluster 0's races, deadlocks and determinism are every cluster's. Not
  symmetric (any of the above fails): falls back to all slices, and says why.
  - Evidence: `fixtures/e_sym` (each bug only in CTA 3: refused and found; good: accepted);
    r2_cublas_gemm symmetric (32 clusters); r2_triton_gemm not (persistent tile loop by
    pid); r2_cute_gemm symmetric.
  - Lost relative to all slices: kernels whose control depends on position (edge tiles,
    persistent schedulers, CLC that runs) get no speedup; overlapping global writes between
    threads are refused even when ordered.
- Status: **argued.** Actions of different CTAs then touch disjoint mbarriers, barriers,
  shared memory and TMEM, so they commute. Their only contact is plain global memory, and a
  race there is found by vector clocks in either order (E-DRF). The state graph is acyclic
  (every action ticks a clock or retires an async op), so no cycle proviso is needed.
  `PTXV_NO_CTA_POR=1` turns it off; the test suite still passes with it on (rung 2).
- If wrong: *miss*, for a cross-CTA interaction through a channel the qualification test
  overlooks.

- **Parked warps released by the candidate** (`sync_ample`, `released_by`): a warp all of
  whose live threads are parked at an mbarrier poll (spin model: blocked until the phase
  completes) takes no step before that phase completes. If no entity other than the
  candidate's own later work (its warp's future async operations; for a pipe completion, the
  later completions of its pipe) can still arrive at that mbarrier, by the learned sets, the
  parked warp's future comes after the candidate and is left out of the conflict check. The
  choice is recorded with those mbarriers' arrival keys as writes, so anyone later learned to
  arrive there forces another round. Debug switch `PTXV_NO_RELEASED`. r2_cute_small: 4% fewer
  states, same verdicts; r2_cublas_gemm: the commit completions that the epilogue's
  accumulator poll blocked become ample.

**Local ample sets (same argument, under E-DRF).** One action alone is expanded if it
commutes with everything:
- a `bar.sync` arrival, unless more threads than the barrier's count may still arrive at it
  (E-BAR-OVER);
- a whole-warp step that starts at an invisible instruction (register, plain-memory,
  async-issue work after a wait);
- a whole-warp `wait_group`, an exit with no pending async ops, or a visible op guarded off
  in every lane;
- the completion of a TMA store or an MMA (data movement; wait_group / commit observe it
  later);
- barrier.cluster arrive / wait (like `bar.sync` arrivals);
- an unguarded exit of *part* of a warp with no pending async ops of its threads (exited
  threads never merge again; an exit commutes with barrier arrivals).
- neither exit rule takes the exit of a CTA's last running threads while another CTA of its
  cluster has a thread that has not exited, or an async op issued in the cluster is pending
  (`exit_ends_reachable_smem`): that exit ends the CTA's shared memory (S-CLUSTER-LIFE), so a
  peer's access to it lands (and may race) before the exit and is a lifetime violation after
  it. MISS 153: `fixtures/e_dsmem_rank` CLUSTER, whose race of the peer's
  `st.shared::cluster` with the CTA's own `ld.shared` the PTX front lost when the exit went
  first. The kernel's instructions are not inspected (SASS reaches a peer through generic
  addresses).
- a split of *part* of a warp on its way out (`exit_bound`): every path its threads can take
  reaches an unguarded exit through invisible instructions only (guards uniform over the
  split and evaluated on current predicates; no uniform-register writes, no warp-collective
  operation), none of its async ops pending. A split it would merge with on the way runs the
  same invisible instructions from there, so merging only regroups invisible steps of threads
  that exit. r2_cublas_gemm: the producer warp drains its 16 stages lane by lane and exits.
  Evidence: `fixtures/e_exitbound` (races on the leaving lanes' path still found; as with
  every reduction under E-DRF, a racy variant may show fewer of its outcomes). Debug switch
  `PTXV_NO_EXIT_BOUND`.

A split also runs through a visible instruction guarded off in every member instead of
stopping there (it is a no-op).

Each action's conflicts are races found in either order. "Whole-warp" matters because a
split that moves can change which splits of its warp merge. `PTXV_NO_LOCAL_POR=1` turns
this off.

**Over-arrivals (both reductions and DPOR).** Arrivals into one mbarrier phase commute only
while the phase gets no more than its expected arrivals before a completion that orders them.
With 4 plain arrivals at a barrier expecting 3, the three that come first complete the phase
and the fourth lands in the next one; which arrival is left over is a scheduling outcome
(`fixtures/mbar_over_arrival`: a race when it is the one after the data write, from separate
warps or from three lanes of one warp step; a count is a special case, `mbar_count_order`).
- **Detection** (exec.rs `rec_late`, `rec_overarrival`, footprint space 25, apart from the
  generation-membership space 18 so that an exact completion is not taken for one): every mbarrier update
  (arrival, complete_tx) reads the key of the phase k it lands in. An update whose actor's
  clock does not cover the completion clock of phase k - 1 (it is not ordered after every
  update of that phase) writes the key of phase k - 1, and so does an arrival of more than the
  pending arrivals at once (an overshoot, a fault). With exactly the expected arrivals per
  phase nothing is written; with an over-arrival every execution writes a key, because the
  arrivals beyond the count are not ordered after the completion in whichever order they come.
- **Stateful explorer:** a plain arrival is no longer a local ample set just because its
  current pending count is greater than its arrival count. Another schedule can complete
  that phase first. Synchronization reduction uses the generation-membership audit below
  and learns the space-25 writes like any footprint. `mbar_plain_generation_order` keeps
  both orders: three plain arrivals target a phase expecting two, and the consumer races
  when the producer's release lands in the next phase.
- **DPOR** stops at the first such update and the stateful explorer redoes the search (a
  note says so; dpor.rs `OVER_ARRIVAL`). Its sleep sets and last-conflict backtracking assume
  that a waiting transition's footprint does not change, which an arrival that would land late
  breaks: the arrival that commuted with the others where it ran is never placed after the
  arrival that completes the phase. That is how DPOR missed `mbar_over_arrival` even with the
  counted-arrival footprints.
- **Before (MISS 125):** the stateful explorer's local rule and DPOR took single arrivals into
  one phase as commuting whatever their number (the counted-arrival footprints cover a count
  only), so the leftover arrival was never placed after the arrivals that complete the phase.
  `fixtures/mbar_over_arrival` good and lanes were clean with the stateful explorer, with
  DPOR and in the `--certify` fallback, on both fronts (the certificate itself refuses them,
  C-PHASE); they are a race (PTX) and nondeterministic (SASS) now (model: ptxv runs before and
  after the fix). Placement: strict; the PTX rule lets any of the arrivals be the leftover one,
  and no hardware assumption enters.
- **Imprecision with S-MBAR-SCOPE (2026-11-11):** the completion clock is the phase's landed
  clocks (`Mbar::done_land`: each update's thread, and an async unit's own clock), and an
  actor's clock covers them only through synchronization. A wait that observes a phase without
  synchronizing with all of its updates leaves the waiter's next update of that mbarrier
  flagged as late, although the waiter's own observation of the same mbarrier orders that
  update after the completion (per-location coherence). Two cases: a `.cta`-scope wait on a
  phase that another CTA's multicast TMA completed, and an async unit's own landing clock,
  which a waiter records in `Thread::landed`, not in its clock. The flag is sound (the
  stateful explorer decides, without the local rule) but costs time: `fixtures/r1c_cluster`
  good falls back on both fronts, and the DPOR test `r1c_good` takes 35.9 s where int7 takes
  7.9 s (`r1c_b13_cluster_lifetime` 20.5 s vs 7.2 s; the quick suite's test binaries, one
  node); the PTX halves `r1c_good_ptx` and `r1c_b14_no_mbarrier_init_fence_ptx` are
  full-tier tests for that reason. Not done: letting a wait's observation of a phase cover
  that phase for the waiter's later updates of the same mbarrier.
- **On the order of events (2026-11-12, MISS 118):** an update whose clock does not cover the
  landed clocks is late only if its order clock does not either (`order_vc_of`: the clock with
  every restricted happens-before the actor holds, `Cover::Order` included; for an async unit,
  what its issuer held at issue). Since MISS 118 and 119 the clock of the issuer of a
  cp.async.mbarrier.arrive or bulk copy reaches the waiters as an order of events only, while
  the landed clocks keep the issuer's epoch, so every later update of a thread that waited for
  such a phase looked late: every round of a producer with several issuing lanes. An order of
  events is a real order (a wait that observed the phase, an async operation after its
  issuer's earlier instructions), so an update ordered after the completion that way cannot
  land in the earlier phase, and the flag stays sound. Test
  `mbar_late_updates_judged_by_the_order_of_events`, source mutant `mbar-late-memory-clock`.

**Synchronization reduction (persistent sets, same argument).** A whole-warp step is also
expanded alone when its *synchronization footprint* conflicts with nothing another entity
can still do (`explore.rs` `sync_ample`). Entities are warps, plus each warp's async units.
- **What a footprint holds:** TMEM allocator, CTA exit, bulk groups, grid gates, strong
  accesses, and mbarrier keys. Plain memory and TMEM data are left out, because their
  conflicts are races (E-DRF).
  - An arrival into phase k reads key (M, k); the arrival that completes phase k also writes
    (M, k+1). This alone does not establish that two actions land in the same phase; the
    membership key below covers both single and counted arrivals. The pending-count keys of
    space 16 are recorded as well (the union of the two policies is a coarser dependence
    relation, so either one's commutations that the other forbids are not taken):
  - Counted arrivals (space 16,
    `rec_count`): every arrival into phase k reads the phase's pending-count key, and an
    arrival of several at once (a count, or a remote operation carrying several lanes) that
    takes the last pending arrivals writes it, so it conflicts with every arrival into its
    phase (DPOR found the count-first order of `fixtures/mbar_count_order` on the PTX front
    only by chance without it).
  - Transaction counts (`rec_tx`): a pure increment (expect_tx without an arrival, local, or a
    remote one landing; cp.async.mbarrier.arrive's raise of the pending count) made with an
    arrival pending reads every last-arrival key of the phase, and the arrival that takes the
    last pending arrival writes the key of its own tx increment (`rec_count`, `mbar_last_keys`);
    made with none pending, the increment writes the phase's count key. Every decrement
    (complete_tx of a thread, a TMA / bulk copy, st.async, a CLC response, cp.async's
    transaction unit) reads the count key; one that leaves a deficit d (tx -d) with an arrival
    pending also reads the last-arrival keys of the increments below d, and with none pending it
    writes the count key. An increment does not commute with the last arrival (with tx 0, that
    arrival first completes the phase, and after it the increment no longer commutes with the
    decrements) nor, once no arrival is pending, with a decrement (the decrement first takes tx
    to 0 and completes the phase early). A decrement with deficit d does not commute with a last
    arrival whose increment is below d (that arrival first can complete the phase, and after it
    the decrement still takes tx below 0). The deficit depends on the tx changes made before the
    decrement, so a decrement that takes tx below 0 with an arrival pending also writes the
    phase's under key, which every other tx change made with an arrival pending reads: the
    orders of those changes that change d are explored (MISS 273, `probes/dpor_tx_level`,
    `tx_level_po`, `txfuzz`: with decrements of 4 and 8 against a last arrival of increment 8,
    the order 4, 8 leaves d = 4 and the order 8, 4 d = 12; DPOR, and on tx_level_po this
    reduction too, ran only the first and reported only the deadlock). Nor does a decrement
    below 0 commute, once no arrival is pending, with another
    decrement (tx 4, decrements of 8 and 4: the 4 first completes the phase early, the 8 first
    never lets it complete; `probes/dpor_tx_overdec`, `sync_tx_overdec_tma`: for a while such a
    decrement only read the keys, and DPOR, and on the TMA case this reduction too, reported
    only the deadlock order; MISS 268 for the TMA case on int7). A copy that lands before its
    producer's arrive.expect_tx covers it commutes with that arrival: `fixtures/c_smm_nvf4` SASS
    needs 164508 states, and took more than 3 million while every last arrival and every
    decrement below 0 shared one key. Other decrements commute with each other. While an arrival
    is pending, increments and decrements commute: `fixtures/s_ptx_cute_ops` (64 threads, each
    raising and completing one transaction unit) needed 268 DPOR states, where writing the count
    key on every increment ran past 300 s (166 before the key). Until 2026-11-12 they recorded
    nothing of the kind, and DPOR, whose over-arrival fallback needs the late update in the
    order it runs, never ran the decrement first (MISS 231; `probes/dpor_tx_commute`,
    `dpor_tx_commute_async` TMA / CLC, `dpor_tx_commute_remote` SASS: DPOR [clean] against
    [nondeterministic, race(, violation)]). The stateful explorer branched on those orders
    already.
  - **Generation membership** (space 18, `memory-write::barrier::arrival_batch_writes`):
    effects are summarized after the complete action. A membership key is read-only only
    for an audited, nonempty batch of arrivals with no transaction delta, completion, fault
    or invalidating effect, whose total is at most half the initial pending count. Such batches stay in the
    same phase in either pairwise order. Other batches write the key. Transaction-count
    changes conflict even with zero arrivals: `expect_tx` can prevent the completion that
    `complete_tx` would otherwise publish. `mbar_transaction_generation_order` pins the
    deadlock reachable in that order; `mbar_plain_generation_order` pins the release race.
  - A poll while the current phase is k reads (M, k), and the completion of phase k writes it.
    Init and inval write every key of M. So a consumer's poll is independent of everything
    except the one completion that would change its result.
  - TMEM alloc / dealloc stay in (space 3) although they also clear the TMEM race shadow.
    They check that shadow first (S-TCGEN05), so a TMEM race with them is found in either
    order too.
    DPOR's footprints also have the mark write every word of the range (space 2, which a
    tcgen05.ld / st of the word reads): the allocation state decides whether that access is
    a tmem-unalloc violation. Until 2026-11-12 only the allocator key was recorded, and DPOR
    lost the violation of a dealloc racing an STTM / LDTM (MISS 233;
    `probes/dpor_tmem_dealloc` NOFREEWAIT SASS: [race] against [race, violation]).
- **What "can still do" means:** every footprint seen during the search, keyed by entity and
  start pc. For a warp, that is the pcs reachable in the CFG from where its live threads are.
  For async units, it is the issue pcs reachable from where the issuing warp's threads are,
  plus the issue pcs of its pending operations. A call may return, and a return may go
  anywhere. Two things are added to what was executed:
  - **Blocked steps.** In every state, a blocked split adds what may have disabled it or will
    enable it (`blocked_sync`): a blocked try_wait reads every key of its M, a blocked poll
    loop reads its flag (space 10/11), and a blocked alloc writes the allocator. This is
    DPOR's "next transition of a disabled process".
  - **Polls, for every phase.** A poll learned at a pc reads every key of its M, not only the
    phase it saw. The phase it reads depends on the phase, which the chosen step may change.
- **Learned sets, then a final check.** The sets are seeded by 16 random complete executions
  and then learned while the search runs. A set can grow by something that conflicts with the
  footprint of an action already chosen (for another entity). Then that choice may have been
  wrong, and the search runs again with the larger sets. Findings and outputs of every round
  are kept, since every transition is a real step. Growth that conflicts with no choice cannot
  change any choice, because conflict distributes over union.
- **Seed walks and the budgets.** The seed walks stop at the search's budgets (the memory
  budget, the time budgets of `--time-budget` and `--mutate-budget-seconds`) before their
  next step. A cut seed set is the set of fewer or shorter walks (as `PTXV_POR_SEED_WALKS`
  or the 1,000,000-step cap give), which the argument below does not use; the verdict is
  marked incomplete anyway, with a note naming the walks (`seed_learned`; test
  `seed_deadline.rs`).
- **Soundness argument.** Take the final round, and a wrong choice `a` with no wrong choice
  after it (the graph is acyclic). Below `a` the reduction is right, so every maximal
  execution that starts with `a` is explored up to reordering. Some execution has another
  entity `e` reach, without `a`, a step `c` that depends on `a`. Run `a` first: the steps
  before `c` commute with `a`, so `e` still reaches `c`'s pc, with the same registers.
  - If `c` is still enabled, `e` later runs a step from that pc, or stays blocked there. A
    later poll may see another phase, which is why polls are learned for every phase.
  - If `a` disabled `c`, `e` is blocked at that pc: `blocked_sync` records it.

  Either way the round learns a footprint at (`e`, pc) that conflicts with `a`. If it was
  learned before the choice, `a` was not chosen. If after, the round is rerun. This is the
  persistent-set theorem; the state graph is acyclic, so there is no cycle proviso. It relies
