      least what R's synchronized with (the earliest member acquires the least). Failed
      iterations of E are invisible, whatever values they read and wherever E leaves the loop.
    - Every other event is decided by the existing conditions (C-PHASE ... C-CAS, C-WARP),
      which R satisfies, as in E-WELLSYNC.

    So every execution has the outcome of one run of the search; the runs agree, so the
    verdict is theirs. Termination: in E every blocking point is R's; a counter wait exits on
    every value at or after the first it exits on, and the counter's last write is an event of
    R, hence of E, so under E-SPIN's fairness (a blocked poll eventually reads the latest
    write) the wait exits; every other wait is decided as in E-WELLSYNC. One terminal run per
    choice sequence gives termination of every fair schedule.

    Why not one run with a taint check. A taint rule "the observed value may reach only loop
    bounds over slots and the next poll of the counter" is unsound with explicit-flow taint:
    a batch counter (`n++` per batch, stored at the end) is never data-dependent on the
    observed value, yet differs between chunkings (fixture e_ring R7). With implicit flows
    taken into account it refuses DeepEP: in dispatch's receiver
    (`intranode::dispatch`, sass:0x3cf0..0x8010) the slot-to-warp assignment is relative to
    the observed head (`R13`), each warp's TMA mbarrier parity flips once per slot the warp
    copies (`R37`), and the output offset is the sum of the observed batch sizes (`R27`). The
    per-slot effects are the same under every chunking, but showing it takes relational
    reasoning across threads. C-RING therefore runs each chunking and compares. The ownership
    facts (each slot written before the tail release that covers it, read after an acquire
    that observed it, reused only after the head release that covers it) are what the race
    detector checks pairwise, on every payload byte, in every run.

    Cost: one run per sequence of choices, at most the product over rings of 2^(w-1) for w
    tail writes. r4b dispatch: 4 runs (two of its four rings have two tail writes); DeepEP at
    3 tokens per ring and chunks of 1 (agent W's `r4c_nowrap`): 256 runs, 9 min.

    Evidence. `crates/sim/tests/wellsync.rs`:
    - `fixtures/e_ring` (one GPU), `e_ring2` (two GPUs, the ring in the consumer's memory, as
      DeepEP lays out its channels) and `e_ring_warp` (DeepEP's consumer shape: a warp-level
      poll by lane 0, a shared-memory relay, the slots of each chunk shared by two warps),
      PTX and SASS: the good variants certify (4 runs, one dropped), and their outputs equal
      exhaustive exploration's (`certified_outputs_match_exploration`).
    - Mutants (`ring_mutants_are_refused_with_their_reason`), each refused: R1 publish before
      the payload write, R2 a read past the observed tail, R3 reuse without the head wait, R5
      the tail released at too narrow a scope, R6 a relaxed tail store, W1 two warps copying
      one slot (all races in some run of the search); R4 a threshold branch on the batch size
      and R7 a batch counter (not chunking-oblivious). The explorer gives each its expected
      class.
    - `e_spin_smem` SP6 (a flag set to 1 then 2, the value stored) is now refused by C-RING
      as not chunking-oblivious (it was C-POLL's refusal).
    - r4b in group mode: dispatch certifies (docs/rung4.md).
  - **C-WARP.** Lane membership: an instruction whose effect depends on which lanes run it
    together runs with lanes that became ready at that pc in one event (an instruction run
    by lanes that were already together, or a barrier / BSYNC / WARPSYNC release: then they
    meet there in every schedule). Lanes the model merged only because they stood at the
    same pc (they arrived by different paths) stay apart until such a release (until
    2026-11-09 any instruction a merged split ran joined them: MISS 30,
    fixtures/e_lockstep_nobsync NOBSYNC certified while GB300 differs). In the certificate's
    run the E-LOCKSTEP join of a SASS load, store or atomic joins only lanes that share a
    token (`lockstep_groups`; the lanes of one atomic step are in lane order only within
    one token), and a BSYNC joins only lanes its BSSY recorded in one step with one token
    (`bsync_groups`): lanes merged at the BSSY may run it apart in another order, and
    E-BSYNC then releases a part alone. So the run's clocks stay below every order's, and
    loads, stores, atomics and BSSY by merged lanes need no membership condition. Where more lanes joining
    would change it too (SASS lane collectives, `BRA.U.ANY`, TMEM collectives and uniform
    operations, which run once per lane group; PTX elect / vote / redux / R2UR / BSSY /
    tcgen05.alloc), runs of the same pc by other lane groups of the warp must be HB-ordered
    with it (they cannot meet there in another schedule). SASS per-lane memory and
    synchronization instructions need only the first part (more lanes only add E-LOCKSTEP
    happens-before); SASS lane-local arithmetic, branches and EXIT need neither. PTX
    `.aligned` ops skip the first part (the explorer waits for all live lanes), and so do
    PTX `redux.sync` / `vote.sync` / `match.sync` whose membermask names the whole warp
    (2026-11-09: the explorer waits for every live lane there too; before, a full-mask
    `redux.sync.max.f32` reached through an if / else failed the certificate.
    probes/redux_f32_paths: 16 warps, 8 min / max [.abs] [.NaN] forms over lanes from both
    sides of a branch, GB300 = both fronts bitwise). BSYNC parks
    only lanes BSSY recorded. A WARPSYNC/BSYNC release need not wait for the order of an
    exited lane's exit: an exit after the arrivals re-checks the release
    (`exit_warpsync_release`, E-BSYNC) and frees the same lanes with the same joined clock
    (an exit adds none). Before 2026-11-06 the certificate required the exit HB-before
    every arrival and refused ptxas's `@P0 EXIT` inside a BSSY region
    (`fixtures/e_bsync_exit`, GB300 output as expected; certified outputs equal the
    explorer's).
    SASS `BREAK` needs neither part (2026-11-06): it clears each executing lane's own bit of the
    warp's convergence mask and releases the lanes parked at that barrier's `BSYNC` once every
    lane still in the mask is parked, joining only the parked lanes' clocks (E-BSYNC). Bit l
    changes only through lane l's own `BSSY` / `BREAK` or a release lane l is parked in, so the
    mask, the release point and its clocks do not depend on how the breaking lanes are
    grouped. Triton's predicated-store chains reach `BREAK.RELIABLE` from two paths
    (fixtures/e_brk; tests/reductions.rs keeps its verdicts and those of its two mutants).
  - **Residency.** The run has every CTA resident (E-RESIDENCY). A cross-CTA wait is decided
    only under that assumption: the certified verdict of a kernel with a poll loop on global
    memory, on a GPU running more than one launch unit, carries the E-RESIDENCY note, and the
    certificate refuses under limited residency or co-tenant mode. `residency::analyze` uses
    the certificate the other way round: its order-independence makes the launch-set search
    exact.
  - The run reports **no finding** (race, deadlock, violation, fault, unmodeled, trap)
    except exit-time `contract` findings (E-BULK-EXIT: an HB check at the end, and every
    schedule's clocks contain the run's, so the run reports the union): a race breaks the
    value argument, and the rest are left to the explorer. Schedule-free
    findings (SASS scoreboard, E-SPIN shape) are added as in exploration. PTX `elect`:
    one run per leader policy (E-ELECT).
- Argument: let R be the run, E any execution. Induction over E: each actor's next event
  in E is its next event in R, with the same outcome and a vector clock ⊇ R's. Values: plain
  reads read the HB-latest write (R race-free; the detector is precise, below, and E has
  at least R's HB edges), strong reads are ordered with every write (C-ORDER) or are CAS
  links that read from R's predecessor (C-CAS), allocator results and warp collectives are
  determined (C-ORDER, C-WARP). Synchronization: C-PHASE
  puts every operation in its run phase (it cannot run before phase k-1 completes, and
  phase k cannot complete without it), so completions join the same clocks; C-WAIT and
  C-GEN fix what waits observe. Progress: each blocking event's enabling condition depends
  only on events before it in R, and every event that could disable it is HB-after it
  (C-WAIT's h), so the R-first event E has not executed is enabled: E continues until it has
  executed exactly R's events, reaching R's final state. So every schedule terminates with
  R's outputs and no finding. With C-RING polls whose observed value steers the program,
  R is one run per sequence of choices, and E follows the run of its own choices (C-RING's
  argument).
- Detector precision (the value step above needs it): the run's race detector reports every
  pair of conflicting accesses that R's HB does not order, unless both are strong and morally
  strong (S-SCOPE). Vector clocks give that only if the per-byte shadow keeps every earlier
  access a later one could race with. `Machine::access_x` drops an earlier access e at a
  write w only when w *covers* e: e is HB-before w, and every access that races with e races
  with w. That holds when w is plain, or when both are strong, in one CTA, and w's scope is no
  wider than e's (moral strength with w then implies it with e). A strong write covers no
  plain access, and an unordered strong pair is kept (`Sh::hw` for writes, `Sh::r` for
  reads); an unordered pair with a plain side is reported. A read replaces only the same
  actor's reads of at least its strength. FastTrack's single last-write epoch broke this:
  warp 0's plain `STS` init followed by its own `ATOMS` became the strong `ATOMS` alone, and
  the other warps' unordered atomics were morally strong with it. The certificate called
  that clean while GB300 was wrong 200/200 (soundness-harness miss 1, `fixtures/
  e_cert_fasttrack`, `tests/wellsync.rs` `plain_write_hidden_by_own_atomic_is_a_race`).
- Where: `crates/sim/src/wellsync.rs`, `wellsync/ring.rs` (C-RING); hooks marked `wellsync.rs` in `exec.rs` (`exec`,
  `mbar_atomic`, `mbar_maybe_complete`, `bar_try_release`, `cluster_try_complete`,
  `warpsync_release`, `access_x`) and the `Machine::wlog` slot (empty, unhashed, dropped by
  clones). `--slices`: per cluster, then the cross-cluster check of E-CTA-INDEP (a certified
  slice's run touches exactly the bytes every schedule touches).
- A failed certificate's unforced runs are executions of the model: a race one of them
  reports (unless the run had LDS/STS plain and `smem::strong_race` may dismiss it) is
  printed (`certificate run race (...)`) and added to the verdict of the exploration that
  replaces the certificate when that exploration does not complete (`run_races`,
  `merge_run_races`; `tests/wellsync.rs`
  `certificate_run_race_survives_an_incomplete_exploration`). C-RING runs with forced reads
  do not count.
- Cross-check (opt-in, `PTXV_CERT_CROSSCHECK=K`, default off): after the certificate holds,
  K runs under seeded random schedules (`explore::random_run`, every enabled action, no
  reduction). A run that reports a finding the certified verdict lacks, deadlocks (no thread
  or unit can step before the run is over), or ends with outputs the certified run did not
  produce (not checked for C-TICKET-ADDR's permuted rows) refutes the certificate, and the
  launch is explored. Findings compare by (kind, signature), except races: by the pair of
  accesses whichever ran first (a signature names the earlier access and the direction),
  `race-dead` equal to `race` (the certificate marks its races after its run, the random runs
  do not). A run stopped with threads still able to step (max(8 x the certificate's steps,
  100000) steps, or a repeating fault) proves nothing by itself, since uniform random choices
  can starve a thread: the deterministic scheduler continues it for as many steps, and a
  continuation that deadlocks, does not terminate, reports a finding the verdict lacks or
  ends with other outputs refutes; one that ends like the certified run adds a note to the
  verdict. The refuting finding is a witness (a
  feasible execution): it is added to that exploration's verdict even when the exploration
  completes without it, with a note (`merge_witnesses`), since a complete exploration that
  lacks it has a reduction or a schedule-dependent check that missed it. A guard against
  checks that fire only at schedule-dependent points (MISS 30, 33, 35); it samples, it does
  not prove. On the MISS 33 shape before its fix (a remote `st.shared::cluster` into a CTA
  that exits without a cluster barrier) it refuted the certificate within 4 random
  schedules, and the witness also corrected the exploration, whose local reduction commuted
  the target CTA's exit with the store (`tests/wellsync.rs`
  `cert_crosscheck_keeps_certified_fixtures`: no refutation of a sound certificate).
  `cert_crosscheck_deadlocking_schedule_refutes` pins MISS 52 at the strict level: on
  probes/warpsync_pairs (SASS) a random schedule switches between the splits of a warp
  between a uniform-register write and its read (the model's splits share the warp's uniform
  registers) and deadlocks, while GB300 runs the probe to completion; the GB300 profile drops
  that switch (E-HW-SPLIT-UR) and certifies it.
- Time budget (`ptxv check --time-budget`, `membudget::time_budget_spent`): a certificate
  run it stops gives a reason ("the certificate's run stopped at the time budget"), so the
  certificate does not hold; a dead-read rerun (`probe_run`) it stops marks nothing dead; a
  certificate that ends after the budget is spent is refused as well, whatever stopped
  (`certify_inner`); and so is one whose cross-check the budget stops. A cut certificate is
  never a pass: the launch is explored, under the same spent budget, and the verdict is
  incomplete (`tests/seed_deadline.rs` `certificates_stop_at_the_time_budget`,
  `crates/cli/tests/time_budget.rs`).
- Evidence: `crates/sim/tests/wellsync.rs` runs the certificate on every fixture variant
  and both front-ends: a certified verdict must equal the expected (exhaustive) one, and on
  a representative subset the certified output equals the exhaustive explorer's unique
  output.
- Status: **argued** (checked against the fixture suite).
- If wrong: *miss* (one run would hide a schedule-dependent bug). The conditions refuse
  rather than approximate: any doubt fails the certificate and the explorer decides.

## S: memory and synchronization semantics

### S-MBAR · code
**mbarrier semantics:** phase counter, pending-arrival count, signed tx-count; a phase
completes when pending = 0 and tx = 0; `try_wait.parity p` succeeds when the phase with
parity p has completed (so parity 1 succeeds immediately after init).
- Where: `exec.rs` mbarrier ops, `try_wait_result`, `complete_tma`.
- Status: **validated.** r0 B01 hangs on GB300 as predicted (tx never reaches 0), and the r0
  B02 hang mode reproduced under witness replay. Bitwise agreement holds on all good kernels.
- Arrival counts (2026-11-07): `mbarrier.arrive [a], count` (SASS
  `SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64.ART0` / `.RED.ART0`, the count in a register) subtracts `count` from
  the pending count at once; a count above the pending count is a fault. probes/mbar_count
  (register and immediate counts, shared::cta and shared::cluster addresses, phases
  completed by one or two counted arrivals; test_wait after each step): GB300 50/50
  scrubbed, both front-ends bitwise; its `over` variant (3 arrivals with 2 pending) is an
  unspecified launch failure on GB300. A remote counted arrival in flight (S-REMOTE-INFLIGHT)
  is delivered as `count` single arrivals.
- `mbarrier.expect_tx` / `complete_tx` (2026-11-08; SASS `SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64.RED.A0TR` /
  `.A0TX`, `.A0T1`): no arrival, the tx-count raised / lowered (it may go negative), the phase
  completing when pending and tx are both 0. They are relaxed (PTX ISA): they publish only
  what the thread's last fence released (`membar_vc`), unlike an arrival. Before, the model
  joined the issuer's whole clock, so a store published by a bare complete_tx was not a race.
  On another CTA's mbarrier (SASS `.RED.A0TX` in CUTLASS / cuBLAS kernels) the issuer's whole
  clock was joined until 2026-11-09 (for the cluster-lifetime check); that check now counts
  the observed landing (S-MBAR-SCOPE), and the update is relaxed there too. The PTX front
  refuses that case at run time (unmodeled). probes/mbar_expect_tx (register / immediate tx,
  shared::cta and shared::cluster addresses, tx below 0, test_wait per step; a fence then
  complete_tx publishing a shared store): GB300 50/50 scrubbed, both front-ends bitwise; its
  `relaxed` variant (no fence) is a race on the PTX front (clean on SASS: S-SMEM-STRONG).

### S-MBAR-SCOPE · code
**An mbarrier wait synchronizes only with the updates of the observed phase it is morally
strong with.** Each update of a phase (arrive, expect_tx / complete_tx, an async unit's
complete-tx or arrive-on) is a strong read-modify-write of the mbarrier with a scope; the wait
is a strong read with a scope. A successful wait acquires an update's release only when the
two are morally strong (same CTA, or both at `.cluster` scope; PTX ISA 8.7) and the
release's scope includes the waiter (8.8, 8.9.4). Any other update still counts toward the
phase, so the wait returns, but it orders nothing. Before 2026-11-09 every update of the
phase was joined into every waiter (the PTX front ignored the wait's scope; the SASS front
has none), so a 2-CTA hand-off through a `.cta`-scoped remote arrive was certified.
- PTX: `mbarrier.arrive` defaults to `.release.cta`, `try_wait` / `test_wait` to
  `.acquire.cta` (9.7.15.16.16, .19); `.relaxed` updates release only what the thread's last
  release fence released, at the narrower scope (release pattern, 8.8), and a relaxed wait
  acquires at the next acquire fence. expect_tx / complete_tx are relaxed.
- Async units: the complete-tx of cp.async.bulk{.tensor} / cp.reduce.async.bulk{.tensor} is a
  `.release` at `.cluster` scope (9.7.10.28.4.1-2, 9.7.10.28.5.3-4) of the copy's own memory
  operations (8.9.1.1, MISS 119 below); tcgen05.commit's arrive-on is at
  cluster scope (9.7.18.12.1); st.async's complete-tx (9.7.10.12, which states no semantics for it) is modeled the same way. Which thread
  performs it is not stated (9.7.15.16.9: the completion "of the asynchronous instruction
  ... initiated by the executing thread"). The model attributes it to the issuing thread
  (R-ISSUER), so a `.cta` wait in another CTA does not pair with it. `ptxv check` reruns a
  PTX check with races as if it were performed in the mbarrier's CTA
  (`Launch::async_mb_dest`); a race that is gone there is a `contract` finding
  (`twolevel::mbar_async_contract`).
- `fence.release.sync_restrict::shared::cta.cluster` releases, at cluster scope, the thread's
  operations on its own CTA's shared memory only; `fence.acquire.sync_restrict::shared::cluster
  .cluster` acquires for shared-memory operations only (9.7.15.4). Restricted
  happens-before is a separate per-thread clock (`Thread::vc_sh`, `Cover`) that orders only
  shared-memory accesses (of one CTA, or of all), carried by mbarrier updates, `bar.sync`,
  `barrier.cluster` and async operations issued after it; strong stores / atomics do not
  carry it (a possible false alarm, never a miss). Other `sync_restrict` forms are refused.
- Observation order (8.9.2) runs through the mbarrier's read-modify-writes only along morally
  strong pairs: a `.cta` update by the waiter's CTA coherence-after a cluster-scope update of
  another CTA cuts the latter's release from the wait. The model joins per update, whatever
  the order of the updates in the phase (the explorers' reductions commute arrivals of one
  phase); a phase that holds both is reported as a `contract` finding (`mbar-chain:<pc>`).
  Not reported: a release of the waiter's CTA cut by a later `.cta` update of another CTA.
- SASS (ptxas 13.0, sm_103a, `-arch=sm_103a`; every PTX form compiled and disassembled):
  - `SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64[.RED].A1T0` is emitted, with nothing before it, for
    `.release.cta`, `.relaxed.cta`, `.relaxed.cluster` and the default arrive, local or
    remote. It is therefore a cluster-scope update that releases at CTA scope.
  - `.release.cluster` adds `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA; MEMBAR.ALL.GPU; ERRBAR; CGAERRBAR` before it:
    a relaxed cluster-scope update after a release fence (8.8).
  - `fence.release.sync_restrict::shared::cta.cluster` is `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA;
    FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`: before an arrive, `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` releases the CTA's shared
    memory at cluster scope.
  - `SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64[.TRYWAIT]` is emitted for `.acquire.cta`, `.relaxed.cta`,
    `.relaxed.cluster` and the default; `.acquire.cluster` adds `CCTL.IVALL` after a
    successful wait; `fence.acquire.sync_restrict::shared::cluster.cluster` is nothing. A
    bare PHASECHK is therefore a cluster-scope wait that acquires the CTA's own updates
    fully and another CTA's for shared memory only; `CCTL.IVALL` acquires the rest.
  - `.A0TR` / `.A0TX` (expect_tx / complete_tx) release nothing of their own, local or
    remote (until 2026-11-09, a remote one joined its issuer's whole clock).
- The copy's own writes (2026-11-11, MISS 119): before, the complete-tx of a `cp.async.bulk`
  (`.tensor` included: every TMA load, SASS `UTMALDG` / `UBLKCP`) released the issuing
  thread's whole clock at issue and what the issuer held for SM-local memories
  (`mbar_note_async`), so a waiter was ordered after every access of the issuer before the
  copy. PTX ISA 9.5 8.9.1.1: "The implicit mbarrier complete-tx operation that is part of all
  variants of cp.async.bulk and cp.reduce.async.bulk instructions is ordered only with respect
  to the memory operations performed by the same asynchronous instruction, and in particular
  it does not transitively establish ordering with respect to prior instructions from the
  issuing thread" (9.7.10.28.4.1 makes it a `.release` at `.cluster` scope; 8.9.1.1 bounds what
  it orders). Now it releases the copy actor's epoch only (`mbar_note_async_own`). The copy is
  still "ordered after prior instructions in the same thread" (8.9.1.1), so the issuer's clock
  at issue, and what it held for SM-local memories, stay as an order of events (`Cover::Order`:
  the certificate's phase checks and S-CLUSTER-LIFE use it, the race detector does not).
  `fixtures/e_bulk_ctx_release`:
  thread 0 stores a word, arrives with `mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx` and issues a 16-byte
  `cp.async.bulk` completing on the mbarrier; thread 32 waits and reads the word. RELAXED (a
  relaxed arrive), AFTER (the store between a release arrive and the copy) and GLOBAL (RELAXED
  with a global word) were clean on both fronts, with `--certify` and DPOR; they are races on
  the PTX front with all three. SASS: ptxas emits the same `SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64` for the
  relaxed and the release arrive, a release at CTA scope on the SASS front, so RELAXED is clean
  there; AFTER's race is reported by the plain-LDS/STS pass and cleared by the strong re-check
  (S-SMEM-STRONG); GLOBAL's `STG`, which ptxas schedules after the arrive, races. good (the
  store before a release arrive) stays clean; NOWAIT (no wait loop) is the positive control.
  Test `bulk_complete_tx_releases_only_the_copy`, source mutant `bulk-ctx-whole-clock`. GB300
  0/1000 runs, plain and scrubbed (2026-11-11), while NOWAIT fails (1/1000 plain, 1000/1000
  scrubbed): a measured null, which discharges nothing. Placement: strict (ISA text), so both
  levels. tcgen05.commit's arrive-on and st.async's complete-tx, outside 8.9.1.1's list,
  still release the issuer's clock at issue. Consequences in the fixtures (model): without
  the order of events, `r1c_cluster` good lost its SASS certificate (C-WAIT: rank 0's wait on
  `peer_empty` was ordered before rank 1's next arrive there only through the multicast's
  complete-tx); with it, it keeps it. A peer CTA's paired alloc is no longer ordered before
  the leader's MMA in `r1c_2sm` and the two fixtures built on it (E-PAIR, PTX front only;
  since MISS 179 the paired alloc is a rendezvous, which orders it).
  DPOR on `r1c_cluster` explores more (fewer events are ordered by memory): the tests
  `r1c_good`, `r1c_b13_cluster_lifetime` and `r1c_b14_no_mbarrier_init_fence` take 34.8 s,
  26.8 s and 41.3 s where the build before took 27.9 s, 22.5 s and 28.4 s (one machine, 8
  threads).
- Consequences: the PTX ISA's fixed forms (cluster-scope arrive and wait; st.async with an
  expect_tx arm at cluster scope; sync_restrict release + relaxed cluster arrive; relaxed
  cluster wait + sync_restrict acquire) are clean on both fronts. A `.cta`-scoped arrive or
  wait across CTAs is a race on the PTX front. On the SASS front it is a race when the arrive
  is bare (no release fence before it). A fence.acq_rel.cluster before a `.cta` arrive, or a
  `.release.cluster` arrive with a `.acquire.cta` wait, is the SASS of a PTX-correct
  hand-off (shared-memory data): clean on SASS, race on PTX.
- 2-CTA pipelines that hand a stage (shared memory or tensor memory) back to the other CTA
  with a bare `.release.cta` remote arrive (`tcgen05.fence::before_thread_sync`, then
  `mbarrier.arrive.shared::cluster`) give the stage's readers no order before the other
  CTA's next writes: a race on the PTX front, and on the SASS front unless a release fence
  (`MEMBAR.ALL.GPU` / `CGAERRBAR`, or `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` for shared memory) precedes the arrive.
  These are load-buffering shapes when the reads have completed by then; no hardware rule
  relaxes them yet (as E-READ-DONE, opt-in). The reads have completed only if the reader
  waited for them before the hand-back: `tcgen05.wait::ld` (PTX), a wait on the LDTM's write
  scoreboard (SASS, S-TCGEN05). A `tcgen05.wait::ld` after the arrive leaves them in flight:
  fixtures/e_tblk_late (ptxas waits on the LDTM scoreboard after the bar.sync that precedes
  the arrive, so the other warps' reads can still be outstanding at the hand-back): a race
  on the SASS front, whatever the scopes. Until 2026-11-12 the SASS front completed an LDTM's
  read at issue and called its ACTA variant clean; until MISS 105 the PTX front's
  `tcgen05.fence::before_thread_sync` released the un-waited `tcgen05.ld` reads (S-TCGEN05)
  and gave `good` contract only.
- Cluster lifetime: a waiter that observed a phase saw its updates land (`Thread::landed`),
  even when it did not synchronize with them; S-CLUSTER-LIFE and async-after-exit count that
  as ordered before its exit, as the joined clock did before.
- Observed, not synchronized (`Cover::Order`): a dropped update still enters the waiter's
  `Cover::Order` clock (`Thread::vc_sh`), and the update's landing enters `Thread::landed`.
  An Order edge carries real-time observation order and no memory visibility: it covers
  no location, so the race detector, C-ORDER, the fence-acquire replays and E-RACE-DEAD
  never see it. The argument: a wait that observed a phase completion returns after the
  completing arrive was performed; that arrive was performed after the arriving thread's
  earlier instructions issued (in-order issue, E-WARP-ORDER); every instruction the waiter
  issues after the wait issues after the wait returned. So an event at the head of an
  Order edge happens later in real time than every event at its tail, which is all that
  event-order arguments use. Readers: `Machine::order_vc` in the wellsync certificate
  (E-WELLSYNC: C-WAIT / C-PHASE, which phase a wait can observe; C-GEN, the `bar.sync` /
  `bar.arrive` and `barrier.cluster` arrival order; the TMEM allocator event order in
  C-ORDER), and `landed` in `observed_by` (S-CLUSTER-LIFE, async-after-exit). A
  scope-insufficient hand-off is therefore a race, not a refused certificate.
  `bar.arrive` does not block: its arrival is counted at issue (PTX ISA, `bar.arrive`:
  the arriving thread does not wait), so its clock holds only what the thread observed
  before issuing it, and an arrive the thread performs later in program order cannot be
  in it.
- Audit `PTXV_MBAR_SCOPE_LOG=1`: every update a successful wait drops for want of scope is
  logged to stderr (kernel, wait pc, CTAs, scopes).
- SM-local happens-before (a SASS PHASECHK's acquire of another CTA's release, `Cover::OnSm`)
  covers tensor memory, for the waiting thread's own accesses and for the asynchronous
  tcgen05 operations it issues afterwards: an MMA or tcgen05.cp checks its TMEM accesses with
  its issuer's `vc_sh` at issue (`AsyncOp::sh`, `tmem_block`), as tcgen05.ld / st do
  (`tmem_access`). Until 2026-11-10 `tmem_block` ignored it: 2-CTA kernels whose leader
  waits with `.acquire.cta` for the peer's hand-back reported false races on SASS
  (fixtures/e_tc_handback ACTA).
  - Which SM: `OnSm` is not one SM's memory. It is the memory the SM's L1 does not cache:
    shared memory (DSMEM included) and tensor memory of every CTA of the cluster
    (`Cover::covers` is true for any CTA's shared memory and for TMEM). What a PHASECHK
    without `CCTL.IVALL` does not acquire is global memory, whose stale lines only
    `CCTL.IVALL` drops. A `cta_group::2` MMA issued by the leader reads and writes the peer
    CTA's TMEM on the peer's SM; the join applies to those accesses as it already applies to
    the same MMA's A-operand reads of the peer's TMEM (`tmem_access`) and to tcgen05.ld / st
    of any CTA's TMEM. It is SASS-only: the PTX front's restricted happens-before comes from
    `sync_restrict` fences and `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA`-style releases (`Smem`, `SmemOf`), which
    cover no TMEM.
  - Hardware runs, a non-discriminating bound, not evidence for the order (probes/tc_handback,
    GB300, 74 pairs = 148 CTAs x 128 threads per launch; good, RCTA and NOWST 200x1000 +
    20000x1000 + 2000x20000 runs x rounds = 4.5e9 pair-rounds each, EARLY 1.6e9, ACTA
    2000x20000 = 2.96e9): the peer CTA waits on `done` with a PHASECHK and no `CCTL.IVALL` and
    then reads (tcgen05.ld) the D half the leader's MMA wrote into its TMEM; ACTA runs the other
    direction (the peer's reads, then the leader's MMA after a leader PHASECHK with no
    `CCTL.IVALL`). Every variant gave 0 wrong words, including RCTA, EARLY and NOWST, which the
    model calls a SASS race: the runs do not separate an ordered hand-off from an unordered
    one, so they bound the rate of a wrong word under this launch and timing and support
    nothing more. Only EARLYD (EARLY with a 5 us sleep, 200x1000 = 1.5e7 pair-rounds) is
    wrong, in every run (9472 words), before and after the ACTA runs.
- GB300 hardware model (two-level check): a wait acquires every update it observed, at any
  scope (E-HW-L1), and MEMBAR.ALL.GPU delivers in-flight remote stores (E-HW-REMOTE-MEMBAR):
  scope races are latent there unless a remote store is still in flight at the arrive.
- Fixtures: e_tc_handback (2-CTA TMEM hand-back: good, RCTA, ACTA, ACTANW, ACTAE), e_mbar_scope (hand-off:
  good, PFC, PFCW, PFCA, FEN, FRC, STA, STAC, NOF, PCTA), e_mbar_mailbox (good, MB, MBNF, MBCA),
  e_mbar_restrict (good, NOF, RLX, GM, GMF).
- Where: `exec.rs` `mbar_rels`, `mbar_async_rel`, `mbar_note`, `mbar_acquire`,
  `acquire_pending_mb`, `sh_vc`; `twolevel.rs` `mbar_async_contract`; PTX `mbarrier.*`,
  `fence.*sync_restrict*`; SASS `SYNCS.*`, `MEMBAR`, `CGAERRBAR`.
- Status: **argued** (PTX ISA 9.5 text; ptxas lowering). Hardware: a stale read of the
  `.cta`-scoped hand-off (weak remote store, `fence.proxy.async.shared::cluster`,
  `.release.cta` remote arrive, `.acquire.cta` wait) was measured on GB200 by others
  (reported, not reproduced here). GB300 (probes/mbar_scope, CUDA 13.0, 2026-11-09): the
  same hand-off without the proxy fence, or with `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta`, read the
  stale slot (15-40 of 3.04e6 hand-offs per configuration without DSMEM noise, each in a
  cluster's first round); with `fence.proxy.async.shared::cluster` (SASS `MEMBAR.ALL.GPU`
  before the arrive) 0 of 1.9e8; with `fence.acq_rel.cluster` 0 of 1.9e8; cluster-scope
  arrive and wait, and st.async, 0 of 6.7e7 each. GB300 did not show the GB200 failure of
  the exact sequence; the PTX front reports it (8.7), and the SASS front too, since no
  measured rule says `MEMBAR.ALL.GPU` drains remote stores (S-REMOTE-INFLIGHT).
- If wrong: *false alarm* if hardware orders a bare remote `SYNCS.ARRIVE` for the issuer's
  own shared-memory accesses (a GB300 rule could then relax the SASS front), or if the PTX
  ISA meant an async complete-tx to be performed in the mbarrier's CTA (the contract
  findings would go away); *miss* if `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` before an arrive does not release the
  CTA's shared memory at cluster scope, or if a bare PHASECHK does not acquire another CTA's
  shared-memory writes (the ptxas lowering of the sync_restrict fences says both do).

### S-MBAR-MEM · code
**An mbarrier can be initialized by a plain `STS.64` of the encoded state word:**
low = (2^20 − n) << 1, high = (2^20 − n) << 11. This is ptxas's lowering of `mbarrier.init` on
a divergent path.
- **Bit 63 is the initial phase parity** (`SYNCS.EXCH.64` or plain store): cuBLAS starts its
  "empty" barriers with it set, so the first parity-0 wait passes (`probes/mbar_phase1`: with
  bit 63 patched into ptxas's init words, every try_wait result flips; counts unchanged).
  Phase 0 then counts as completed at init.
- **Over a live object** (no inval since its init), an aligned 8-byte store of a state word
  re-initializes it as `mbarrier.init` / `SYNCS.EXCH.64` does: ptxas lowers a per-thread-address
  `mbarrier.init` to `STS.64` of the word (+ `SYNCS.CCTL.IVALL`), adding `SYNCS.CCTL.IV` only
  when the PTX invalidated first. The re-init races with the old object's init and atomics it
  is not ordered after, forgets its waits (`mbar_reset_seen`) and starts the new count and
  phase. Any other store over a live mbarrier, and on the PTX front every plain store over
  one, is a `violation` (contract: PTX requires `mbarrier.inval` before the object's memory is
  reused; from the ISA text as remembered, not checked offline); the object stays. Model and
  contract only: what GB300 does with such a store is not measured. Until 2026-11-12 the store
  left the old object (count, phase, waits): the SASS front missed the race and the deadlock
  the PTX front reports for the same kernel, and both fronts called a plain store over a live
  mbarrier clean (MISS 218; fixtures/e_mbar_sts_live, probes/mbar_sts_live).
- **Independent of the order the run took** (since 2026-11-12, MISS 241). Liveness at the
  store depends on its order against the object's init and inval, which plain stores do not
  fix: they run eagerly inside a step (E-DRF), a split at them can be ample, and the
  certificate runs one order. So a store over the bytes, or an init, not ordered with the
  object's inval or init reports in either order, by happens-before as a race does: an inval
  leaves its epoch (`Machine::mbar_dead`) until the next init at the address; a later store
  not ordered after it is the violation above (on SASS, a state word over the whole object:
  a race of the init with the inval), and so is an init not ordered after it (a race); an
  init with no live object checks the bytes' last plain write, which must be ordered before
  it (else the violation, or on SASS for a state word a race of two inits). Before, MISS 218's
  check saw only the order explored: a store unordered with the inval of the object, or with
  its first init, was clean on SASS exhaustive and on both fronts with --certify, and an
  STS.64 re-init unordered with the inval was a missed race (fixtures/e_mbar_store_order,
  probes/mbar_store_order); the commit's own "residual" note said only --certify after an
  inval, which understated it.
- Follow-ups of 2026-11-12 (RMK4's review of MISS 241's fix):
  - the init with no live object checks every write the shadow keeps for the 8 bytes, the
    earlier ones in `Sh::hw` too, not only the last (`Sh::w`): a plain store then a strong one
    by the same thread, unordered with the init, was clean (fixtures/e_mbar_hidden_write SWAP,
    STRONGS; srcmut mbar-init-hidden-write);
  - its happens-before is the shared-memory-only one (S-MBAR-SCOPE), as `store_over_mbar`'s:
    an inval ordered before the init only through shared memory was a race
    (fixtures/e_mbar_init_restrict good, INITP; srcmut mbar-init-restrict);
  - every mbarrier operation reads the object's (re)initialization key (footprint space 15),
    which init and inval write: the synchronization reduction took an inval and an
    `expect_tx` / SASS `SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64.RED.A0TR` (which read neither a phase key nor
    the pending count they change) as independent and ran the update first only, so the
    update of an invalidated object was clean (a regression of MISS 242's fix;
    fixtures/e_mbar_inval_vis EXPTX, EXPTXS on SASS; srcmut mbar-inval-key-atomic;
    polls and waits read a phase key, which the inval writes, so they already conflict);
  - an mbar-store finding is confirmed by the plain model as a race is
    (`explore.rs` `needs_plain_rerun`): with value-insensitive polls (E-POLL-ANY) a reuse
    ordered by `st.release` / `ld.acquire` after the inval was a violation where the
    synchronization reduction is off (`PTXV_NO_SYNC_POR`, or any kernel with
    `st` / `ld.shared::cluster`; fixtures/e_mbar_reuse_ordered good, STX, CL; srcmut
    mbar-store-plain-rerun);
  - SASS `SYNCS.CCTL.IV` and init are lane-join points (E-LOCKSTEP).
  - A SASS state word over an invalidated object, not ordered after the inval, is reported
    by `store_over_mbar` as an init racing with the inval. The default explorer runs a plain
    store that can go before the inval before it (E-DRF), and then the store is the init of a
    live object that the inval races with; the dead-object path sees only a store that cannot
    run before the inval (fixtures/e_mbar_reinits FLAG: it reads a relaxed flag set after
    the inval; srcmut rmk4-dead-sass-word).
- Open (registered, not fixed):
  - MISS 256: writes by async units (TMA, cp.async, st.async), atomics and stmatrix over a
    live mbarrier; a SASS weak DSMEM `ST.E` into another CTA's mbarrier (S-REMOTE-INFLIGHT:
    `complete_remote_op` applies it as a plain access, unchecked at issue and at landing: over
    DSMEM, a store unordered with the inval is clean on SASS in every explorer, and one
    unordered with the first init is clean under --certify); the shared-memory write of
    `tcgen05.alloc`'s result over a live mbarrier; the response `clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel` writes.
  - MISS 265: two `STS.64` inits of one object by two warps, unordered, are clean on SASS in
    every explorer; the PTX front reports the race (fixtures/e_mbar_double_sts_init good,
    PREINV).
  - MISS 266: an object initialized by `STS.64` revives after its inval: with no live
    object, `mbar_decode_mem` / `mbar_materialize` decode the state word still in memory, so
    an arrive after the inval runs on a fresh object (fixtures/e_mbar_resurrect good, INV2
    on SASS).
  - MISS 272: a poll whose result is discarded is lifted to a NOP on SASS (ptxas emits
    `SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64 PT, …`; `crates/sass/src/lib.rs`), so a discarded test_wait /
    try_wait on a never-initialized or invalidated object is clean on SASS where PTX reports
    the violation (fixtures/e_mbar_discarded_poll good, INV; USED, which keeps the result,
    reports on both fronts). The SASS rows of e_mbar_inval_vis TWAIT, TWAITS, TRYW, TRYWS
    (uniform init: no state word to revive) and e_mbar_resurrect WAIT are this, not MISS 266
    (RMK4's second review, G1).
  - MISS 267 (liveness): `mbarrier.test_wait` / `try_wait` on an invalidated object never
    finishes under DPOR, and for some kernels under --certify (no verdict within 120 s;
    fixtures/e_mbar_inval_vis TWAIT, TWAITS, TRYW, TRYWS on PTX, TWAITU on both fronts,
    e_mbar_resurrect WAIT on PTX; the same for a never-initialized object,
    fixtures/e_mbar_discarded_poll on PTX and USED on SASS); the stateful explorer and the run
    with no reductions report the violation.
  probes/mbar_explorers pins these rows (the classes each explorer reports while the miss is
  open, so a change in a column the miss does not explain is a difference); it runs every
  mbarrier memory fixture in each explorer (exhaustive, DPOR, --certify, no POR).
- Where: `exec.rs` `mbar_decode_mem`, `MbarInit`, `MbarInval`, `mbar_init`, `store_over_mbar`,
  `mbar_store_unordered`; the stores that can re-initialize read the old atomics, so
  `explore.rs` `mbar_init_pcs` counts SASS 8-byte shared stores as init pcs
  (`forget_dead_sync`; fixtures/e_mbar_forget_initpcs, srcmut mbar-sts-init-pcs).
- Status: **validated** (r1a bitwise = GB300; r2_cublas_gemm bitwise = GB300). Count and
  phase bit decoded. The re-initialization over a live object: ptxas output only.
- **Reduction dependencies:** ordinary shared writes, including partial writes and async
  landings, can create an encoded barrier before `mbars` contains an entry. In a kernel
  that observes barrier memory, those writes and operations that drain them are scheduling
  points. Synchronization footprints write every overlapping eight-byte barrier's init,
  phase and arrival keys; learned releases also track initialization. Invalidating a
  materialized barrier can expose its encoded backing word again and is visible too.
  A specifically diagnosed uninitialized query reads its resolved eight bytes and all
  phases in full DPOR footprints. Distinct invalid queries then commute; init, invalidation,
  shared stores and completions retain conflicts. Blocked-query footprints include every
  active lane's resolved target and all phases. Other query errors and synchronization-only
  error footprints remain universal dependencies. Query execution still reports once and
  parks without changing predicates or acquiring anything.
  Status: **argued and tested**, against unreduced schedule graphs on both frontends in
  `barrier_materialization`; this is not a proof of native POR soundness.

### S-TCGEN05 · code
**tcgen05 ordering (PTX front-end):**
- `tcgen05.ld` executes as a per-thread actor whose view advances only at
  `fence::after_thread_sync`;
- `fence::before_thread_sync` releases that view, except the thread's `tcgen05.ld` reads
  since its last `tcgen05.wait::ld` and its `tcgen05.st` writes since its last
  `tcgen05.wait::st` (2026-11-12, MISS 105; `exec.rs` `tc_released`, also in the
  E-TC-FENCE-NOP rerun's implied fences). PTX ISA 9.7.18.6.4.4: "the producer threads that
  issue the asynchronous tcgen05 instructions must explicitly wait for the instructions'
  completion before synchronizing with the consumer threads"; 9.7.18.8.5: `wait::ld` /
  `wait::st` block "until all prior tcgen05.ld [st] operations issued by the executing
  thread have completed". The cut is by the actor's clock (loads and stores share it), at
  the first access not waited for: a waited access issued after it is held back too until
  that wait (conservative). Fixtures: e_tblk_late `good` (race on PTX; before, contract
  only), probes/tc_handback NOWST (no wait::st: race on PTX; before, contract);
- `tcgen05.dealloc` (2026-11-12, MISS 111) is the thread's own synchronous event, after its
  earlier tcgen05 operations that have completed (`tc_released`), not after a `tcgen05.ld` /
  `st` it has not waited for: PTX ISA 9.7.18.6.1, asynchronous instructions "are not
  inherently ordered with respect to other tcgen05 operations in the same thread (unless
  pipelined)", and the only pipelined pairs with ld / st are `ld -> wait::ld` and
  `st -> wait::st`. Before, the dealloc was an event of the thread's tcgen05.ld/st actor,
  whose clock covered every earlier load and store of the thread. Fixture
  e_dealloc_unwaited (LDNW, STNW: race on PTX; on SASS STNW races, LDNW is ordered by the
  scoreboard wait ptxas puts before the dealloc);
- MMA and commit share one in-order pipe per issuing thread;
- a commit releases every earlier op of that pipe;
- (rung 2) `tcgen05.alloc` / `dealloc` / `relinquish_alloc_permit` are synchronous: the
  thread itself performs them (PTX ISA 9.7.18.6: only mma/cp/shift/ld/st are asynchronous);
- an alloc or dealloc writes every word of its columns: an access of those words that is not
  ordered with it is a race, whichever comes first (`tmem_mark`). Allocs and deallocs do not
  race with each other;
- a warp-wide `tcgen05.alloc` reached by a warp whose lanes are all guarded off is not
  executed by it and does not wait on the allocator (Triton's `@p tcgen05.alloc` with
  p = tid < 32, reached by four warps: before 2026-11-08 the other three warps blocked there);
- (rung 2) a thread's asynchronous tcgen05 ops are ordered after its own earlier
  instructions (the actor's clock includes the thread's clock at issue);
- (rung 2) `tcgen05.st` is asynchronous like `ld`; `wait::st` completes the stores for the
  same thread's later tcgen05 ops. Another thread sees them through `wait::st`,
  `fence::before_thread_sync`, a synchronization, and `fence::after_thread_sync` (the
  `wait::st` part since MISS 105).
- (2026-11-08) "The same thread's later tcgen05 ops" include its MMA pipe (`tcgen05.mma` /
  `cp` / `shift`): `wait::st` / `wait::ld` order the thread's completed `tcgen05.st` /
  `tcgen05.ld` before the asynchronous tcgen05 operations it issues afterwards, with no
  `tcgen05.fence` (`exec.rs` `tc_wait_orders_pipe`; before, only its later `tcgen05.ld` /
  `st` were ordered, and the PTX front reported a race between a thread's own `tcgen05.st`
  of the A operand and its later `tcgen05.mma` in the mslk mx8mx4 grouped GEMM).
  PTX ISA 9.7.18.6.1: `.wait::*` are synchronous tcgen05 instructions, "inherently ordered
  with respect to other tcgen05 operations" of the thread, and `tcgen05.st -> tcgen05.wait::st`
  is implicitly pipelined (9.7.18.6.2.1); 9.7.18.6.4.2 ("Non-pipelined instructions, same
  thread") orders `st; wait::st; ld` with no fence, and the fence in its example 2 follows an
  mbarrier wait, not a tcgen05.wait. GB300 (`probes/tc_st_mma`, 296 CTAs x 2000 iterations
  per mode, 9.47M words each): an MMA issued by the storing thread right after its own
  `STTM` read the new words in every case, as C and as A in TMEM, with and without the fences
  and also with no `wait::st` (so the probe shows the hardware order but cannot separate
  wait::st from issue order). The SASS front already orders them (STTM is the thread's own
  scoreboarded access), so `sass_gb300` needs no profile item. Stores by other threads of
  the warp or CTA still need the fences (the remaining mx8mx4 PTX races).
  Fixture `s_tc_st_mma` (clean; the MMA issued before `wait::st`: race).
- SASS `STTM` (2026-11-12, MISS 107): its tensor-memory write is an event of the thread's
  STTM actor (`Machine::sttm_actor_id`, the fifth fixed actor per thread), ordered after
  everything the thread has seen, that enters the thread's clock (and its MMA pipes') only
  at its `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.T`, ptxas's lowering of `tcgen05.wait::st` (`Op::TmemWaitSt`); a
  converged warp's lanes are joined after the fence (E-LOCKSTEP, MISS 149), so an elected
  lane's later release carries every lane's completed writes.
  Before, the write was complete at issue: an STTM in flight at a `BAR.SYNC` was ordered
  before the next writer of its columns (the reviewer's STNW: SASS clean while round 2's MMA
  overwrote D). The STTM's register read scoreboard says nothing about the TMEM write and is
  not used. An STTM ordered after the thread's earlier LDTMs only by the TMEM queue is a
  contract finding at both levels (E-TMEM-QUEUE, not assumed); a later
  LDTM of the thread sees its own STTM only after the `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.T`.
- SASS `STTM` / `LDTM` are scoreboarded and modeled as the thread's own accesses, except that an
  `LDTM`'s tensor-memory read completes only when its write scoreboard is waited (2026-11-12;
  before, at issue): the read is an event of the thread's tcgen05.ld/st actor, ordered after
  everything the thread has seen, that enters the thread's clock at a control-word wait on that
  scoreboard (the consumer's or any other instruction's) or a `DEPBAR.LE` that leaves it
  complete. TMEM loads complete in issue order (L-OPREAD), so such a wait completes every
  earlier LDTM too, including one with no scoreboard; a later `STTM` of the thread follows its
  LDTMs only once they completed (an order through the TMEM queue alone: a contract finding at
  both levels, E-TMEM-QUEUE). Until then the thread's
  releases (bar.sync, mbarrier arrives) do not carry the read: an LDTM waited only after the
  hand-back races with the next writer of its columns (fixtures/e_tblk_late). Where: `exec.rs`
  `ldtm_issue` / `ldtm_complete`, `Kernel::ldtm_sb` / `ldtm_waits` (sass lift).
- One `.cta_group` per kernel (2026-11-12): PTX ISA, tcgen05: "All tcgen05 instructions
  within a kernel must specify the same value for the .cta_group qualifier." A kernel whose
  tcgen05 instructions name both (PTX `tcgen05.*.cta_group::N`; SASS `UTC*` with or without
  `.2CTA`, except `UTCATOMSWS.AND`, the same for both) is a `violation` (`cta-group-mix:`,
  `explore::cta_group_mix`, a static finding on both fronts). ptxas 13.0 refuses such a kernel
  ("uses single CTA(.cta_group::1) and CTA pair granularity(.cta_group::2) and that is not
  allowed"), so the SASS front sees one only in an edited binary; `ptxv check --front ptx`
  checks it without a cubin. `tcgen05.commit.cta_group::N` tracks only the thread's earlier
  operations of group N (PTX ISA, tcgen05.commit): a thread's operations of the group other
  than its first one's go to a second pipe (`Machine::pipe2_actor_id`, `Thread::pipe2_vc`,
  its own FIFO), unordered with the first. Before, one pipe and every commit tracked both.
  Fixture `e_cta_group_mix` (C2: a cta_group::2 commit after cta_group::1 MMAs, violation
  and race; D2: a cta_group::2 dealloc, violation).
- Where: `exec.rs` `tc_actor`, `pipe_actor`, `push_async`.
- Status: **argued, medium confidence.** It follows the PTX ISA's examples. On GB300 the
  fences are NOPs (B06 is invisible), so hardware cannot confirm the rule.
- Races the fences would order are reported as contract findings (E-TC-FENCE-NOP).
- If wrong: either direction.
- Retire: a tcgen05 litmus campaign.

### S-TC-COLLECTOR · code
**`tcgen05.mma .collector::a::{use,lastuse}` computes with the A operand read from memory
(its descriptor, or TMEM), and is a `contract` finding unless a still-valid
`.collector::a::fill` of the same A precedes it.** PTX ISA (tcgen05 MMA, collector usage):
fill keeps A in the tensor core's collector buffer; use / lastuse "can be read from the
collector buffer" and require a previous fill that is still valid; lastuse, discard and an MMA
without the qualifier (= discard) let the buffer go; reuse is opportunistic (the core may
reload), so the source memory must not change while the MMA has not completed.
- Model: per CTA (the issuing CTA of a `cta_group::2` pair), the collector holds the
  fingerprint of the A operand of the last fill (as read at its completion, in the issuing
  pipe's order) or nothing. A use / lastuse reads A from memory (race-checked as any MMA
  operand read) and reports `mma-collector-unfilled` (no valid fill) or `mma-collector-stale`
  (A differs from the filled A): D then depends on whether the core reuses or reloads. use
  keeps the buffer, lastuse / discard empty it. In a kernel that uses the qualifiers, every
  MMA also writes the collector state (DPOR footprint space 24), and two MMAs of one CTA
  issued from different pipes without an order (vector clocks, as for a race) are
  `mma-collector-unordered`, so one run finds a schedule-dependent collector in either order
  (probes/tc_collector m6, model only).
- SASS: ptxas 13.0 encodes fill / use / lastuse as `gdesc[URa].A_KEEP` / `.A_REUSE.A_KEEP` /
  `.A_REUSE` on the A operand of `UTCHMMA` / `UTCQMMA` / `UTCOMMA`; any other suffix is
  refused. `.collector::b::*` (`.ws` only) and `.ashift` stay refused.
- Where: `ptx` `lower_inst` (tcgen05 `mma`), `sass` UTC*MMA lift, `exec.rs`
  `collector_a` (called by `complete_mma` / `complete_mma_lp`), `Tmem::coll_a`.
- Status: **validated** (probes/tc_collector, GB300 2026-11-09, 100 runs per variant, both
  front-ends bitwise): `good` (fill, use, lastuse on unchanged A) equals the plain MMAs. In
  all five contract-breaking variants GB300 read A from memory: A rewritten (with
  fence.proxy.async) after the fill completed, another A descriptor, use with no fill, use
  after lastuse, use after a discard. The model's outputs equal GB300's in every variant.
  No variant made GB300 serve stale collector data, so the finding rests on the ISA's
  permission to reuse, not on an observed reuse.
- Evidence classes: the output semantics of contract-keeping sequences are hardware-measured.
  That violations are nondeterministic is argued from the ISA.
- If wrong: *miss* only if hardware reused a collector across an A change that the
  fingerprint does not see (it covers every A element the MMA reads); a *false alarm* if the
  ISA meant use to be well defined after a discard.
- Retire: never (an ISA contract).

### S-TMA · code
**TMA semantics:** N-D tiled box, innermost dimension contiguous in smem, then the
shared-memory swizzle (none / 32B / 64B / 128B: XOR of address bits [4,4+B) with [7,7+B));
SWIZZLE_* MMA descriptors address the same layout (row r at (r/8)·SBO + (r%8)·span).
Loads zero-fill out-of-bounds elements and complete_tx = box bytes; stores skip
out-of-bounds elements, and their shared-memory source bytes reach nothing, so the model does
not read them (an unwritten clipped row is no S-INIT use; fixtures/e_tma_store_clip: GB300 500
runs plain and 500 with scrubbed memory = the simulator; an unwritten in-bounds row is still
reported).
4-bit maps (`16U4_ALIGN8B`, case `elem4`) are modeled as byte maps (dims and box in bytes) whose
coordinate 0 counts elements, two per byte (an odd one is reported as not modeled). The global
and shared layouts are packed, so the copy is the byte copy. Evidence: r3_cute_mxf4 (CuTeDSL
MXF4, A and B through such maps) equals GB300 bitwise on both front-ends.
With a swizzle, a box whose inner dimension is narrower than the span has each smem row
padded to the span: element (row q, column c) sits at q·max(span, inner bytes) + c·esize before
the address swizzle (`exec.rs` `tma_box_off`); complete_tx still counts the unpadded box bytes.
**im2col mode** (`cp.async.bulk.tensor.<n>d ... .im2col` loads, SASS `UTMALDG.<n>D.IM2COL`;
`.im2col_no_offs` stores, `UTMASTG.<n>D.IM2COL`; `sim/im2col.rs`): the box is `pixels` rows of
`channels` elements, laid out and swizzled as a 2-D tiled box. Pixel q is the start pixel
(the spatial coordinates and n of the instruction) advanced q steps in row-major order through
the pixel bounding box [lower_i, dim_i - 1 + upper_i] of each spatial dimension (innermost
first; past the last one n advances); element (q, c) is the tensor element at channel c0 + c
and spatial coordinates pixel + offset_i. Offsets are unsigned, packed into 16 bits as ptxas
passes them in the UR (rank 5: three 5-bit fields, rank 4: two 8-bit, rank 3: 16 bits).
Out-of-tensor elements read as 0 (loads) or are skipped (stores). An illegal instruction on
GB300 (reported as a fault): a channel start not on a 16-byte boundary, and a store through a
map whose pixel box reaches outside the tensor (lower corner < 0 or upper corner > 0). Not
modeled: a start pixel outside the bounding box or a start n outside the tensor, element
strides, im2col reductions, Im2colWide maps. Evidence: `probes/tma_im2col` (2026-11-08): 48
loads through six maps (rank 3 / 4 / 5; u8 / u16 / u32; corners from -3 to 2; channels past
C; no swizzle / 64B / 128B; the largest offset per rank) and 12 stores through three maps =
an independent Python model and the simulator, bitwise; the fault conditions were found by
single-access variants (each faulting case gave an illegal instruction; aligned starts and
contained boxes did not).
The swizzle phase comes from the shared-memory address, not from the box: a swizzled box may
start at any 128-byte-aligned address (not only at a multiple of 8 rows x span), and element
(q, c) lands at swz(start + q·span + c·esize). A swizzled start that is not 128-byte aligned
faults (reported as `fault`). This is what multicast slices rely on: cuBLAS
`nvjet_sm103_tst_64x8_64x16_2x4_h_bz_TNT` (cluster of 8) has rank 1 multicast rows 4..7 of a
128B-swizzled tile to stage base 0x2400 + 0x200.
Shared-to-shared bulk copies (`cp.async.bulk.shared::cluster.shared::cta.mbarrier::
complete_tx::bytes`, SASS `UBLKCP.S.S [URd], [URs], URn`) are the non-tensor bulk load with the
issuing CTA's shared memory as the source (read by the bulk actor, proxy-checked like a TMA
store's source), landing in the CTA named by the destination's cluster address and completing
its bytes on the mbarrier at URd+1 (`probes/bulk_s2s`: a 2-CTA cluster, each CTA copying 4 KB
to its peer and 4 KB to itself, 20/20 GB300 runs identical, both front-ends bitwise,
`probe_bulk_s2s_matches_hardware`, 2026-11-06).
- Where: `exec.rs` `complete_tma`, `complete_tma_store`, `tma_swizzle_ok`, `swz`,
  `tma_box_off`; `case` `tmap_geometry`.
- Evidence (start alignment): probes/tma_mcast_swizzle (GB300, 2026-11-03). Spans 32/64/128 B
  and starts 0..0x780 in 128-byte steps (48 configs): a cluster-of-4 multicast load
  (rank r loads 4 rows to start + 4r·span on every CTA) and a TMA store both match
  swz(address) in 48/48. The box-relative model (start + swz(offset)) fails every load and
  every store whose start is not a multiple of 8 rows x span. Starts 0x10, 0x20, 0x40 fault with
  "misaligned address" for every span. fixtures/c_mm_bf16_mcast (that nvjet kernel):
  certified (E-WELLSYNC), `hw` 1000/1000 bitwise = simulator, also with smem scrubbed. Before,
  the simulator required (8 x span)-alignment and reported a false `violation`, which
  defeated the certificate; the exploration then ran past 200k states, and `compare` printed a
  false MISMATCH (it compared one explored cluster's output with the whole launch's).
- Status: **validated** for in-bounds 2-D/3-D boxes, no swizzle (r0, r1a) and 128B swizzle
  with TMA store (r1b: bitwise 1000/1000 with smem scrubbed). Narrow inner boxes:
  probes/tma_narrow_box (GB300, 2026-11-03) loads and stores a 16-row u16 box for every
  swizzle (none/32B/64B/128B) and inner width 16..128 bytes: the padded layout matches all 13
  configurations, the dense one fails all 6 with inner < span; fixtures/c_mm_bf16_ttn (cuBLAS
  8 x 16 bf16 box, SWIZZLE_64B) is bitwise equal to the GPU. Out-of-bounds fill/skip is
  **unvalidated** (no fixture exercises it yet; rung 3, B25). Element addresses wrap modulo
  2^64: trtllm-gen's dynBatch output map (fixtures/r3b_trtllm_bmm) has dims 2^31 and a stride
  of 2^35 - 256 that its coordinate 2^30 cancels, and it clips padded token rows with a
  coordinate in an 8-row dimension; the store matches GB300 bitwise.

### S-TMA-2CTA-MCAST · code
**`UTMALDG.<N>D.MULTICAST.2CTA`** (cp.async.bulk.tensor ... .multicast::cluster.cta_group::2;
cuBLAS's 2-CTA nvjet kernels, picked for bf16 M = N >= 512): the box lands at the same offset
in every CTA rank of the ctaMask (UR bits 16..31, as `.MULTICAST`), and each destination's
transaction completes on the mbarrier at the operand's offset in the CTA of the destination's
pair whose peer bit is the mbarrier address's own (CUTLASS's 2SM multicast loads clear the peer
bit: the pair leader's mbarrier).
- Where: `exec.rs` `Op::TmaLoad` (`mask` with `pair`).
- Status: **validated** (2026-11-05) by `probes/tma_2cta_mcast`: cluster of 4, one load of a
  512-byte box by rank 0 with ctaMask 0xf / 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 / 3 / 6, the mbarrier of rank 0 or 1,
  the destination address of rank 0 or 1, with and without `.cta_group::2`; each CTA's
  mbarrier expects 512, 1024, or the model's bytes, and is polled for ~10 ms (168 configs).
  On GB300 the box lands in every masked rank at the destination's offset (the destination
  address's rank does not matter); without `.cta_group::2` each destination completes its
  own mbarrier (the mbarrier rank does not matter); with it, the mbarrier at the offset in
  rank (r & ~1) | (mbarrier rank & 1), so a pair leader's mbarrier gets 1024 bytes for mask
  0xf. Every flag agrees with the rule (an mbarrier that gets fewer bytes than it expects
  never completes; more: either, the transactions can step over zero, not used), and the 56
  configs where every mbarrier expects exactly the model's bytes equal both front-ends bitwise
  (`crates/sim/tests/tma_2cta_mcast.rs`). End to end: the cuBLAS 2-CTA nvjet kernels above
  (E-PAIR) use `UTMALDG.3D.MULTICAST.2CTA` and equal GPU bitwise.
  The same holds for a gather4 box (`UTMALDG.2D.GATHER4.MULTICAST[.2CTA]`, trtllm-gen routed
  GEMM; 2026-11-08): `probes/tma_g4_mcast` gathers rows 5, 30, 7, 5 (256 bytes) with the
  same masks (and 5), mbarrier and destination ranks, with and without `.cta_group::2`, each
  mbarrier expecting the model's bytes (56 configs); GB300 = both front-ends bitwise
  (`crates/sim/tests/tma_g4_mcast.rs`).
- If wrong: *false alarm* (deadlock / tx mismatch on the wrong mbarrier) or *miss* if a
  transaction completes an mbarrier that should still wait.

### S-TMA-GATHER4 · code
**`cp.async.bulk.tensor.2d...tile::gather4 [d], [map, {c, r0, r1, r2, r3}], [m]`** (SASS
`UTMALDG.2D.GATHER4`) loads `box[0]` elements at column c of each of the four rows into shared
memory exactly as a `box[0] x 4` tiled box at d would land (rows in operand order, padded to
the swizzle span, the address swizzle, S-TMA), zero-filling out-of-bounds elements (rows
outside the map or negative, columns past either edge); complete_tx = 4 x box[0] x element
bytes. The map is an ordinary tiled 2-D map with box height 1 (trtllm-gen's token map:
box 128 x 1, u8, 128B swizzle); anything else is reported. A column whose byte offset is not a
multiple of 16 is an illegal instruction on GB300 (reported as `fault`).
- Where: `sass` `UTMALDG` lowering (5 coordinates); `ptx` `.tile::gather4`; `exec.rs`
  `complete_tma`.
- Status: **validated**: fixtures/s_gather4 (six gathers through 128B / 64B / 32B / no-swizzle
  maps, narrow 128B box, rows 64, 1000, -1 and repeated rows, columns -8 and past the right
  edge, destinations at 128-byte offsets not aligned to 8 rows x span) = GB300 1000/1000 on
  both front-ends, and its recorded bytes. Columns 3 and 100 (u16) and 4 (u16, 128B) are
  illegal instructions on GB300 (variant `misaligned`); fixtures/r3b_trtllm_bmm = GB300 bitwise.
- If wrong: wrong shared-memory images of gathered rows (bitwise mismatches).

### S-PROXY · code
**Async-proxy visibility of generic writes.** A generic-proxy store to shared memory
(`st.shared`, cp.async) is visible to a later async-proxy read (TMA store source,
`tcgen05.mma` operand) only if some thread executed `fence.proxy.async` after the store
happened-before it (the writer itself, or a thread that synchronized with the writer), and
that fence happens-before the async operation's issue. Otherwise the result is a proxy race.
- Where: `exec.rs` `proxy_check`, `proxy_wcheck` (each fence's vector clock recorded in
  `Op::Fence`).
- Rung 5: `probes/proxy_fence` answers the open question below. Rung 1b's pipeline with the
  fence moved after the epilogue's barrier, executed by every thread (Triton's order) or only
  by the issuing thread, is correct in 1000/1000 scrubbed runs on GB300; without any fence,
  1000/1000 runs are wrong (994 distinct outputs). Before, a fence by another thread was not
  credited, and Triton's flash attention (`cp.async.wait_group; bar.sync;
  fence.proxy.async; tcgen05.mma`) was a false alarm.
- Status: **validated** (the necessity direction). Rung 1b B04 deletes the epilogue's
  `fence.proxy.async` (in SASS: `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` + `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`); with shared memory
  scrubbed, GB300 writes a wrong output in **1000/1000 runs (61 distinct outputs)**, and both
  front-ends report the proxy race. The sufficiency side is the writer-side formulation
  CUTLASS uses (every epilogue thread fences, then the named barrier, then one thread issues
  the store); the good kernel matches GB300 bitwise in 1000/1000 scrubbed runs. A fence by a
  different thread that happens-after the write is credited too (rung 5 probe above).
- If wrong: *false alarm* if hardware/PTX also credits other threads' fences; *miss* if
  fences need more (e.g. a specific scope).
- Open: closed by `probes/proxy_fence` (see above).
- State spaces (2026-11-06). ptxas on sm_103a: `fence.proxy.async` and
  `fence.proxy.async.shared::cluster` are `MEMBAR.ALL.GPU` + `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`,
  `.shared::cta` is `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` + `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`, `.global` is `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.G`
  alone, and `tcgen05.wait::st` is `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.T` (one per wait in probes/tmem_ldred).
  Only the `.S` forms count for the shared-memory check. `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.G` /
  `fence.proxy.async.global` orders global memory only and covers no check
  (`FenceKind::ProxyAsyncGlobal`); `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.T` lifts as `tcgen05.wait::st`. Before,
  all three lifted as the shared-memory fence, so a `.global` or `.T` fence hid a missing
  `.shared::cta` one. probes/proxy_fence variant `global` puts `fence.proxy.async.global` in
  place of the epilogue's fence (SASS `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.G`, no `MEMBAR`): with shared memory
  scrubbed, GB300 writes a wrong output in 1000/1000 runs (528 distinct outputs), and both
  front-ends report the proxy race.
- Async-proxy writes (MISS 54, 2026-11-11): a TMA load or bulk copy into shared memory needs
  the same fence after the last generic write of each byte it overwrites (`proxy_wcheck`, sig
  `race:proxyw`). Before, only async-proxy reads were checked, so a happens-before order alone
  was clean. GB300 (probes/handoff_window v=11): `STS.128; MEMBAR.ALL.CTA`, a bare remote
  arrive, then the peer's `cp.async.bulk` shared::cluster over the same bytes: the store landed
  after the copy 21 times in 9.88e9 hand-offs; with `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` after the store, 0 in
  4.86e9. Fixture e_mbar_lww (LWWC: SASS race, was clean). A generic *read* before an async
  write: S-PROXY-WAR (a contract finding at the strict level).
- Global memory: S-GPROXY (since 2026-11-09; before, a missing `.global` fence was a *miss*).

### S-PROXY-WAR · code
**Strict level: a generic shared-memory read before an async-proxy write of the same bytes
needs a proxy fence.** The typical case is a consumer that reads a TMA-loaded stage with
`ld.shared` / `LDS` and releases it with an mbarrier arrive. The producer's next TMA load then
overwrites the stage, with no `fence.proxy.async` between the read and the load. The PTX ISA's
proxy-preserved causality order (8.9.5) applies to every conflicting pair, so the strict level
wants a `fence.proxy.async` (by any thread) that the read happens-before and that
happens-before the async op, as S-PROXY does for a write. Without one, `check` reports a
`contract` finding (sig `proxy-war:<read pc>:<async pc>`), not a race. The GB300 profile
discharges it (E-HW-PROXY-WAR), so the row is `ptx_contract: contract` and `sass_gb300` decides
the launch. A read that is not ordered before the async write at all is a race, reported by
the destination access as before.
- Placement history: first an unchecked exemption at the strict level (practice, then probed,
  2026-11-11). Now a strict contract finding, discharged at the hardware level, like the other probe-backed deviations (E-DESC-VERSION, S-TMAP-TAIL).
  Impact, measured over every fixture and kernel_db record before the change: 3 records go
  from clean to contract only (cute.TensorStatsKernelTMA f32.1x5: `LDS.128` at 0x3fd0, then
  `UTMALDG.1D` at 0x4b30; cute.FusedDoubleRMSNormBwd f32.16x20480 and 16x40960: `LDS.128` at
  0x1740 / 0x1760, then `UTMALDG.3D` at 0x0d70). No fixture changed and no certificate changed.
  TMA pipelines whose consumer release reaches the producer through a proxy fence on the
  happens-before path are not affected.
- Evidence class (strict level): the PTX ISA's text (argued). If the hardware needs nothing
  here, the finding is a false alarm at the strict level only; the gb300 level removes it.
- Fixture: e_mbar_lww `WAR` (contract at the strict level on both fronts, clean under the
  GB300 profile); `WARF` (a `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta` after the read: clean at both).
- Where: `exec.rs` `proxy_wcheck`, `proxy_war_check`; `hwprofile.rs` (the discharge).
- Status: **argued** (strict level).
- If wrong: *false alarm* at the strict level (a contract finding only).

### S-GPROXY · code
**Async-proxy accesses of global memory.** A TMA / bulk load, store or add-reduction
(`cp.async.bulk{.tensor}`, `cp.reduce.async.bulk{.tensor}`) accesses global memory in the async
proxy. It is ordered after an earlier conflicting access (a write; for a store or reduction
also a read) only along proxy-preserved base causality order (PTX ISA 8.9.5): the earlier
access is by an async op issued in the same CTA ("same proxy, and by the same thread
block"), or a global proxy fence lies on the happens-before path between them, executed
after the access by its thread or by a thread that observed it, and happening before the
op's issue (as S-PROXY). A generic access needs the fence; so does another CTA's async
access, which after its completion (implicit generic-async proxy fence, 9.7.10.28.2) counts
as generic. The other direction (an async write, then a generic access that observed its
completion) needs nothing.
- Fences that order global memory: `fence.proxy.async.global` (SASS `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.G`),
  `fence.proxy.async` with no state space (every state space; ptxas: `MEMBAR.ALL.GPU;
  FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`), a kernel boundary (8.9.4, API synchronization). Not:
  `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta` / `.shared::cluster` on the PTX front. The SASS front
  cannot tell `fence.proxy.async` from `.shared::cluster` (both `MEMBAR.ALL.GPU;
  FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`) and credits the pair for global memory (`MEMBAR.ALL.CTA;
  FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`, the `.shared::cta` form, it does not).
- Findings: HB-ordered but not proxy-preserved is a `contract` finding (`gproxy`; for two
  add-reductions, atomic per 9.7.10.28.4.2, `gproxy-order`: the order the kernel's
  synchronization means to impose is not guaranteed, e.g. the deterministic accumulation
  shape, a semaphore handed on with st.release / ld.acquire between CTAs whose reductions go
  to one buffer). Contract, not race: the ISA requires the fence, but GB300 showed no failure
  (probes/gproxy). (E-CPASYNC-PROXY is a contract finding too, with no GB300 evidence:
  probes/proxy_cpasync has no positive control, so it is not evidence, not even a measured
  null.) Accesses not ordered by happens-before are left to the race detector; two such
  reductions are a schedule choice as before (N-BULK-RED).
- Where: `exec.rs` `gproxy_check` (from `complete_tma`, `complete_tma_store`),
  `Thread::gfences`; PTX `fence.proxy.async*`; SASS `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.{G,S}`.
- Fixture: e_gproxy (good, NOF, ALL, SH, ST, STF).
- Status: **argued** (PTX ISA 9.5 text; ptxas lowering). GB300 (probes/gproxy, 2026-11-09):
  a thread's generic global stores read back by its own bulk copy were never stale (0 of up
  to 1.2e10 words per variant), fence or not: the necessity is not measured, so the findings
  are contract findings, on both fronts.
- If wrong: a contract finding the ISA would not require if hardware and the ISA order
  async-proxy global accesses by generic synchronization alone; *miss* if
  `MEMBAR.ALL.GPU; FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` does not order global memory (ptxas's lowering of
  `fence.proxy.async` says it does).
- Not modeled: `cp.async` (non-bulk, generic proxy per the ISA), tensor-map reads (S-TMAP),
  multimem bulk forms.

### S-MULTIMEM · code
**NVLS multicast memory.** A case's `[[multicast]]` objects (capture: `cuMulticastCreate`,
`cuMulticastAddDevice`, `cuMulticastBindMem`, `cuMemMap` of the multicast handle) get an
address range of their own; each `binds` entry maps a range of it to a buffer on one GPU.
- `multimem.ld_reduce` (SASS `LDGMC`) loads the bytes from the bound location of every GPU
  and reduces them (N-MULTIMEM). `multimem.st` / `multimem.red` (SASS: plain `STG` / `REDG`
  with the address in the multicast range; `probes/multimem/forms_sass.txt`) store / reduce
  at every bound location. Each per-location access carries the instruction's semantics and
  scope (race detection, release / acquire) and they happen at one step, in GPU order.
- ptxas emits `.STRONG.SYS` for every `multimem.ld_reduce`, `.weak` included; the SASS front
  lifts `LDGMC` as relaxed `.sys`, the PTX front keeps `.weak` as a plain load.
- PTX front: a non-multimem access to a multicast address, or a multimem operation on another
  address, is undefined behavior (PTX ISA 8.2.3) and reported as a `violation`. SASS front:
  `STG` / `REDG` on a multicast address are multimem stores / reductions; any other access
  to one (LDG, ATOMG with a result, TMA) is `unmodeled`. A multicast range a GPU has no
  memory bound at is `unmodeled`.
- Status: **argued**. GB300 (`probes/multimem`, 4 GPUs): `multimem.st` lands in every member
  (`results/st.txt`); concurrent `multimem.red.release.sys.add.s32` from 4 GPUs gives the exact
  count in every member; `multimem.ld_reduce` reads every member (N-MULTIMEM). "At one step" is
  not a hardware claim: the PTX model treats the per-location accesses as independent, in an
  unspecified order.
- Where: `crates/case` `Multicast`; `lib.rs` `build_launch`; `exec.rs` `mc_resolve`,
  `mem_locs`, `Op::LdReduce`, `Op::St`, `Op::Atom`; PTX front `"multimem"`; SASS `LDGMC`.
- If wrong: *miss* of a protocol that observes two members of one multimem store or
  reduction in different orders with relaxed reads (the model lands them together).
- Retire: model each per-location access as its own scheduled event.

### S-VA-ALIAS · code
**Alias proxy between virtual mappings of the same bytes** (until 2026-11-10: S-MC-ALIAS,
multicast / unicast only). A mapping is one virtual address range that reaches an allocation:
the buffer's own (primary) mapping, a multicast (NVLS) mapping, and each further mapping a case
lists in `[[views]]` (a second `cuMemMap` of one handle, a peer's import of an exported
allocation, a legacy-IPC open).
- Rule (model). Two accesses X then Y to the same bytes through different mappings, at least
  one a write: Y is ordered after X only if an alias fence F lies on the happens-before path,
  X -> F -> Y. Alias fences: `fence.proxy.alias` (SASS: L-ALIAS-FENCE); a launch after the
  previous grid on the same GPU completed (stream order); `griddepcontrol.wait` (the
  previous grid completed). X ranges over the byte's retained writes (the last one and the
  unordered strong ones kept besides it) and, when Y is a write, the reads since the last
  write (value-insensitive poll reads included). Otherwise `race:alias`
  (within one address space; across address spaces see below).
  - X and Y not ordered by happens-before: checked only when Y reads X's write (Y may return
    X's value, e.g. an acquire poll of a release made through another mapping; only the
    lenient strong rule below can cover it). An unordered write-after-read or
    write-after-write pair is not an alias race: it has no order to lose, and in the
    schedule with the write first a read pair is read-after-write. This keeps the check
    independent of which access a schedule runs first (until 2026-11-10 an NVLS barrier's
    poll against a peer's next arrival was reported only in the schedules where the poll ran
    first: a false alarm on the fenced Triton barrier).
  - Both strong, same thread: a fence between them in program order (`alias_self`). Every
    strong access since the thread's last fence stays pending (merged byte ranges per
    mapping; never dropped).
  - Both strong, different threads: also ordered when Y's thread executed any
    `fence.proxy.alias` before Y (lenient: the CUDA guide's `red; fence; poll` placement,
    where the fence need not follow X).
  - Two reads never conflict.
  - Asynchronous units: a bulk copy or TMA accesses global memory through the mapping its
    address or tensor map names; the NIC through the primary mapping (its registration).
  - An access to an allocation with several mappings whose mapping the model does not know:
    `unmodeled` (`va-view:<pc>`), never a guess.
- PTX ISA text (9.x):
  - 8.2.2: "Two distinct virtual addresses are said to be aliases if they map to the same
    memory location."
  - 8.6: "Although virtual aliases use the generic method of memory access, since using
    distinct virtual addresses behaves as if using different proxies, they require a proxy
    fence to establish memory ordering." The list of distinct methods includes "accesses to
    the same location via the same proxy using distinct virtual memory addresses".
  - 8.7: two operations are morally strong only if "Both operations are performed via the same
    proxy"; 8.7.1: conflicting operations not related in causality order and not morally
    strong are a data-race.
  - 8.9.5: X precedes Y in proxy-preserved base causality order if they are "performed to the
    same address, using the generic proxy", or "X and Y are aliases and there is an alias proxy
    fence along the base causality path from X to Y". The condition names no direction: it
    covers a read X before a write Y (write-after-read) as much as a write before a read.
  - 8.6.1 (visibility only): strong modifications "eventually become observable" by strong
    accesses through a different proxy at system scope "even if these used distinct memory
    addresses". This makes a poll terminate; it orders nothing.
  - `fence` (9.7.15.4): ".alias of the .proxykind qualifier refers to memory accesses performed
    using virtually aliased addresses to the same memory location"; bi-directional proxy fences
    "take effect within a single thread". The ISA also has `fence.proxy.alias.release.sys` /
    `.acquire.sys` and `fence.alias.sync_restrict::read.release.sys` (PTX 9.5); ptxv does not
    accept them yet (the PTX front refuses an unknown fence form).
- CUDA programming guide, Virtual Aliasing Support: multiple `cuMemMap` mappings of one
  allocation are "proxies"; "writes to one proxy of the allocation are considered inconsistent
  and incoherent with any other proxy of the same memory until the writing device operation
  ... completes"; within one kernel "a fence.proxy.alias can be used between the two accesses".
- Which pairs are aliases:
  - One address space (one process; with UVA that spans its GPUs): two mappings are distinct
    virtual addresses of one location, the ISA's definition. Multicast / unicast, a second
    `cuMemMap`, a single process mapping a peer's allocation at another address. The rule
    applies between any threads of that address space, and between two accesses of one
    thread.
  - Different address spaces (torchrun ranks are processes; case `spaces`): each process uses
    its own mapping, and virtual addresses of two address spaces are not comparable. The ISA's
    definition does not settle it; the guide's "proxy" wording would make every mapping one.
    Default: a finding of kind `alias-xspace` (signature `alias-xspace:<x>:<y>`), graded
